CARDIOVASCULAR__Foundations of CVS:
Overview — Cardiac Cycle
The cardiac cycle = the sequence of mechanical + electrical events in one heartbeat, divided into systole (contraction/ejection) and diastole (relaxation/filling).
The organising principle: blood flows down pressure gradients, and valves open/close passively when the pressure either side reverses — every event follows from "which chamber now has the higher pressure".
Why it matters: the cycle explains heart sounds (valve closure), murmurs (valve disease), the JVP waveform, pulse, and the pressure-volume basis of heart failure — cross-ref valve disease, heart failure, the cardiac action potential note (the electrical trigger).
The Phases — follow the left heart through one cycle

2. Isovolumetric contractionVentricle contracts, all valves shut → pressure rises sharply, no volume changeAll closedVentricular P rising, not yet > aortic

Systole = phases 2–3 (isovolumetric contraction + ejection); diastole = phases 4–5 + atrial systole (relaxation + filling). The two "isovolumetric" phases are the key concept — all valves shut, so the ventricle changes pressure without changing volume, bracketing ejection.

Pressure-Volume Relationships — the conceptual core
  • The Wiggers diagram logic: atrial, ventricular, and aortic pressure curves overlaid with ventricular volume + the ECG + heart sounds — every valve event is where two pressure curves cross
The pressure-volume (PV) loop — one cycle as a loop
  • Filling (mitral open) → isovolumetric contraction (vertical line up) → ejection (aortic open) → isovolumetric relaxation (vertical line down)
  • Stroke volume = width of the loop (end-diastolic volume − end-systolic volume)
  • The loop's shape changes with preload, afterload, contractility (cross-ref the Starling / cardiac output note)
The JVP Waveform — the cycle seen in the neck
The jugular venous pressure reflects right atrial pressure through the cycle:
Wave Cause

c waveTricuspid bulging into the atrium during isovolumetric contraction

Clinical links: absent a waves = AF; cannon a waves = complete heart block; large v waves = tricuspid regurgitation.
Linking Electrical to Mechanical — the trigger
  • P wave → atrial systole
  • QRS → ventricular depolarisation → isovolumetric contraction begins (S1 follows)
  • T wave → ventricular repolarisation → relaxation (S2 around here)
The electrical event always slightly precedes the mechanical one it triggers (cross-ref the cardiac action potentials / ECG note).
Clinical Relevance
  • Heart sounds + murmurs: timing within the cycle localises valve lesions (systolic vs diastolic murmurs)
  • Atrial kick lost in AF → reduced filling → can precipitate failure in a stiff ventricle
  • S3/S4 → heart failure / stiff ventricle
  • JVP waveform → arrhythmias, tricuspid disease, tamponade/constriction
  • PV loop → the framework for preload/afterload/contractility + heart failure (next notes)

Overview — Conduction System & Action Potentials
Two linked ideas: the conduction system (the wiring that spreads the signal in the right sequence) and the cardiac action potentials (the ionic events in individual cells that are that signal).
The decisive distinction: there are two types of cardiac cell with two different action potentials — pacemaker cells (SA/AV node — spontaneously fire) and contractile myocytes (atrial/ventricular — fire when triggered).
Why it matters: underpins the ECG, all arrhythmias, heart block, and the Vaughan-Williams antiarrhythmic classes — cross-ref the ECG note, arrhythmias, the cardiac cycle.
The Conduction System — the wiring
Structure Role
SA node (right atrium)The pacemaker — fastest intrinsic rate (~60–100/min) → sets heart rate
Atrial myocardiumSpread across atria → atrial contraction (P wave)
AV nodeThe only electrical connection atria→ventricles; delays the signal (~0.1s) to let atria empty before ventricles contract (the PR interval)
Bundle of HisCarries signal into the interventricular septum
Left + right bundle branchesDown either side of the septum
Purkinje fibresRapid spread through ventricular myocardium → coordinated ventricular contraction (QRS)
Pacemaker hierarchy: SA node (60–100) > AV node (40–60) > ventricular/Purkinje (20–40) — the fastest sets the pace ("overdrive suppression"); if the SA node fails, a slower escape pacemaker takes over (the basis of escape rhythms in heart block).
The AV nodal delay is the key functional point: ensures atria finish contracting before ventricles start (preserves the atrial kick) and protects the ventricles from very fast atrial rates (AF/flutter).

The plateau (phase 2) is the key feature — Ca²⁺ influx both sustains the AP and triggers contraction (excitation-contraction coupling); it makes the cardiac AP long (~300 ms) so the muscle can't be tetanised (a fibrillating pump is useless).

Defining features: no phase 1, 2 or stable resting potential; upstroke is Ca²⁺-driven, not Na⁺; the slow drift in phase 4 (funny current) creates automaticity. The slope of phase 4 sets the heart rate — steeper → threshold sooner → faster rate (the target of autonomic control + drugs).
Autonomic Control — how rate is modulated
Input Effect Mechanism
Sympathetic (noradrenaline, β1)↑rate (positive chronotropy) + ↑AV conduction + ↑contractilitySteepens phase 4 slope → threshold reached sooner

At rest the vagus dominates (intrinsic SA rate ~100; vagal tone holds it ~70) — which is why atropine speeds the heart, β-blockers slow it (block sympathetic phase-4 steepening), and digoxin ↑vagal tone (slows AV conduction — useful in AF).
Refractory Periods — why the heart can't tetanise
  • The long plateau → a long absolute refractory period: the cell can't be re-excited until repolarised → prevents tetany + summation, and limits how fast the ventricles can be driven
  • The relative refractory period + abnormal automaticity/re-entry circuits are the substrate for arrhythmias (cross-ref)
Linking to the ECG — bridge to the next note
  • SA node fires + atrial depolarisation → P wave
  • AV nodal delay → PR interval
  • Ventricular depolarisation (His-Purkinje) → QRS
  • Ventricular repolarisation → T wave
The conduction sequence and the ECG are the same events viewed differently (the ECG note builds this out fully).
Clinical Relevance
  • Heart block: AV nodal/His disease → PR prolongation (1st) → dropped beats (2nd) → AV dissociation + escape rhythm (3rd/complete) — directly explained by the conduction sequence + pacemaker hierarchy
  • Antiarrhythmics (Vaughan-Williams) map onto the AP phases: I = Na⁺ channel (phase 0), II = β-blockers (phase 4/sympathetic), III = K⁺ channel (phase 3, prolong AP), IV = Ca²⁺ channel (nodal phase 0)
  • Ivabradine = funny-current (If) blocker → slows the SA node specifically (phase 4) → rate control without affecting BP/contractility
  • Hyperkalaemia alters the AP (tall T, broad QRS) because K⁺ governs phases 2–3 (cross-ref electrolytes)

Overview — The ECG Basis
The ECG records the summed electrical activity of the heart from the body surface — it's the conduction sequence + action potentials (previous note) viewed from outside.
The single organising principle: a wave of depolarisation moving TOWARDS a recording electrode = upward (positive) deflection; moving away = downward. Every ECG feature follows from this plus the fixed conduction sequence.
Why it matters: the ECG is how conduction disease, arrhythmias, ischaemia, and electrolyte/drug effects are detected — cross-ref the conduction/AP note (the source), arrhythmias, ACS, electrolytes. This is the physiological basis (how the trace is generated + what each part represents), not a full interpretation tutorial.
How the Trace is Generated — the core concept
  • The ECG measures potential difference between electrodes as depolarisation/repolarisation waves sweep across the heart
  • The towards/away rule: depolarisation towards an electrode → positive deflection; away → negative; perpendicular → biphasic/flat
Why depolarisation and repolarisation can both be upright: depolarisation spreads endocardium→epicardium, but repolarisation goes epicardium→endocardium (opposite direction and opposite charge) → the two cancel into same-direction deflections (why the QRS and T wave are both usually upright).
The leads view the heart from different angles (limb leads = vertical/coronal plane; chest leads = horizontal plane) — each "sees" the same electrical events from its own direction.

Where's atrial repolarisation? Hidden within the QRS (too small to see, masked by the much larger ventricular depolarisation). The PR interval = the AV nodal delay made visible — which is why AV block shows as PR changes. The QRS is large (large ventricular mass); the P wave is small (less atrial muscle).
Reading the Paper — the measurement basis
Standard speed 25 mm/s, calibration 10 mm/mV
  • Small square = 0.04 s (1 mm); large square = 0.2 s (5 mm); 5 large squares = 1 s
  • Rate: 300 ÷ (large squares between R waves) if regular; or count QRS on the rhythm strip × 6 if irregular
  • Normal intervals: PR 0.12–0.20 s (3–5 small squares); QRS <0.12 s (<3 small squares); QTc ~<0.44 s
Axis — the net direction of depolarisation
  • The cardiac axis = the overall direction of the ventricular depolarisation wave (normally down-and-left, ~−30° to +90°, because the large LV dominates)
  • Left axis deviation (LVH, conduction blocks) and right axis deviation (RVH, PE) shift it — detected by which leads are positive/negative (the towards/away rule applied across leads)

The unifying idea: every abnormal ECG is either an abnormal rhythm (where the impulse starts), an abnormal conduction (how it spreads), or an abnormal myocardium (ischaemia/electrolyte/structural changing the AP).

Overview — Starling's Law & Determinants of Stroke Volume
Starling's law (the Frank-Starling mechanism): the more the ventricle is filled (stretched) in diastole, the more forcefully it contracts — so stroke volume rises as end-diastolic volume rises, within limits.
This sits inside the bigger question of what determines stroke volume — governed by three factors: preload, afterload, and contractility. Starling's law is specifically about preload.
Why it matters: the physiological engine behind heart failure, shock, valve disease, and the response to fluids/inotropes/vasodilators — cross-ref the cardiac output note (SV × HR), heart failure, shock, the cardiac cycle (PV loop).
The Frank-Starling Mechanism — the core concept
  • The principle: ↑venous return → ↑end-diastolic volume (EDV) → ↑stretch of cardiac muscle fibres → more forceful contraction → ↑stroke volume
  • The cellular basis: stretching the sarcomere to its optimal length increases the overlap + sensitivity of actin-myosin filaments to calcium → stronger contraction (length-tension relationship)
The functional purpose: it matches output to input automatically — if more blood returns, the heart pumps more out beat-to-beat, without nervous control. It also balances the two ventricles (if the right pumps more, the left receives more and matches it).
The Starling Curve — the graph logic
  • Plot: stroke volume (or cardiac output) vs preload (EDV / filling pressure) → a curve that rises, then plateaus, and eventually falls
  • Rising portion: more filling → more output (the normal operating range)
  • Plateau/descending portion: beyond optimal stretch the fibres are overstretched → contraction weakens — the decompensated heart failure zone
Curve shift Cause Meaning
Up + left↑contractility (sympathetic, inotropes)More SV for the same preload
Down + right↓contractility (heart failure, ischaemia, β-blockers)Less SV for the same preload — needs higher filling pressures for any given output
This is why the failing heart is "preload-dependent" and prone to congestion: it operates on a depressed curve, needing high filling pressures → which back up into the lungs (pulmonary oedema).
The Three Determinants of Stroke Volume
Determinant Definition ↑ by Effect on SV
PreloadThe stretch/filling at end-diastole (EDV) — the Starling factor↑venous return (fluids, lying down, exercise), bradycardia↑SV (up the curve)
AfterloadThe resistance the ventricle pumps against (arterial BP/SVR; aortic valve)Hypertension, aortic stenosis, vasoconstriction↓SV (harder to eject)

  • Preload determinants: venous return, blood volume, atrial kick, venous tone, posture; estimated by CVP / JVP / EDV
  • Afterload key point: ↑afterload → harder ejection → ventricle compensates with hypertrophy (LVH); a failing ventricle is very afterload-sensitive (why vasodilators/afterload reduction help heart failure)
  • Contractility = the steepness of the Starling curve; raised by sympathetic/inotropes, lowered by ischaemia/failure/β-blockers
Putting it Together: Stroke Volume → Cardiac Output
SV = EDV − ESV; CO = SV × heart rate. So CO is governed by the three SV determinants plus heart rate (cross-ref cardiac output note).
Ejection fraction (EF) = SV / EDV (normally ~55–70%) — the clinical marker of contractility; reduced EF = systolic heart failure (HFrEF); preserved EF with poor filling = HFpEF (diastolic).

Overview — Cardiac Output
Cardiac output (CO) = the volume of blood the heart pumps per minute — the central measure of how well the heart meets the body's demands.
The master equation: CO = Stroke Volume × Heart Rate — everything that changes CO works through one of these two terms.
This note is the hub: it takes stroke volume (Starling note) and heart rate (conduction/AP note), combines them, then feeds into blood pressure (BP = CO × SVR). CO is what fails in heart failure and shock, and adapts in exercise, pregnancy, sepsis.
The Master Equation
CO = SV × HR. Typical resting values: SV ≈ 70 mL, HR ≈ 70 bpm → CO ≈ 5 L/min (roughly the whole blood volume per minute). Cardiac index = CO / body surface area (normalises for body size — the clinical measure).

The Stroke Volume Half — recap

  • Ejection fraction (EF = SV/EDV, ~55–70%) = the clinical index of the SV side; reduced EF = systolic heart failure
The Heart Rate Half — recap + the key nuance
  • HR is set by the SA node, modulated by autonomic tone (sympathetic ↑, vagus ↓ — the phase-4 slope, from the AP note)
The crucial nuance — HR and CO are not simply linear: ↑HR usually ↑CO, but at very high rates (fast AF, SVT) diastole shortens → less filling time → ↓EDV → ↓SV → CO can actually fall. There's an optimal heart rate; beyond it, lost filling time outweighs the rate increase — why very fast tachyarrhythmias drop CO and cause syncope/shock.
How CO is Regulated — matching output to demand
  • Autonomic nervous system: sympathetic → ↑HR + ↑contractility + venoconstriction (↑venous return) → ↑CO; parasympathetic → ↓HR
  • The Frank-Starling mechanism: ↑venous return → ↑preload → ↑SV (auto-matching)
  • Hormonal: adrenaline (↑HR/contractility); RAAS (↑volume → ↑preload, longer-term)
Venous return is the often-forgotten driver: CO cannot exceed what returns to the heart — venous return and CO are interdependent (the heart only pumps out what it receives; Starling ensures it matches).

Overview — Blood Pressure Regulation
BP must be high enough to perfuse organs but not so high it causes damage — so it's tightly regulated by short-term (seconds–minutes, neural) and long-term (hours–days, hormonal/renal) mechanisms.
The master equation: BP = Cardiac Output × Systemic Vascular Resistance. Every regulatory mechanism — and every antihypertensive drug — works by adjusting one or both.
Why it matters: the physiology behind hypertension, antihypertensive drug targets, shock, and the response to haemorrhage/standing — cross-ref cardiac output (CO), Starling (SV), hypertension, shock, RAAS/renal physiology.
The Master Equation — everything reduces to this
BP = CO × SVR, where CO = SV × HR and SVR is set mainly by arteriolar tone (the "resistance vessels").

Short-Term — the Baroreceptor Reflex
  • The sensors: baroreceptors (stretch receptors) in the carotid sinus and aortic arch detect arterial stretch (= pressure), reporting to the medulla (vasomotor centre)
The reflex (negative feedback)
  • ↑BP → ↑baroreceptor firing → ↑parasympathetic + ↓sympathetic → ↓HR, ↓contractility, vasodilation → BP falls back
  • ↓BP (standing, haemorrhage) → ↓firing → ↑sympathetic + ↓parasympathetic → ↑HR, ↑contractility, vasoconstriction → BP restored
Key features: fast (seconds), buffers moment-to-moment changes — most importantly on standing (prevents the gravity BP drop; failure → orthostatic hypotension). Chemoreceptors (carotid/aortic bodies) also contribute, responding to ↓O₂/↑CO₂/↓pH with sympathetic activation (mainly in severe hypoxia/ischaemia).
Long-Term — RAAS
The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system controls BP over hours–days by adjusting blood volume + vascular tone — the kidney is the long-term BP controller.

Overview — Vascular System & Haemodynamics
The vascular system is the circuit the heart pumps into — its properties (resistance, compliance, capacitance) determine how blood flows and where pressure is generated/lost.
The organising principle: blood flow is governed by flow = pressure gradient ÷ resistance (the haemodynamic Ohm's law), and each vessel has a specialised job — arterioles set resistance, capillaries exchange, veins store volume.
Why it matters: explains the SVR term in BP = CO × SVR, plus oedema, atherosclerosis distribution, varicose veins, shock, and vasodilators/vasoconstrictors — cross-ref BP regulation, shock, atherosclerosis, oedema/HF.

ArteriolesThe resistance vessels — adjust radius to control flow + BPSet SVR; heavily smooth-muscle-walled
CapillariesExchange of gases/nutrients/wasteThin (one cell), huge surface area, slow flow
VeinsReturn blood; the capacitance vessels — hold ~65–70% of blood volumeLow pressure, distensible, valves
The two most important functionally: arterioles (resistance/BP — the biggest pressure drop) and veins (volume reservoir — venoconstriction shifts blood back → ↑preload).
The Haemodynamic Equation — flow, pressure, resistance
Flow (Q) = ΔP / R (pressure gradient ÷ resistance) — the master relationship.
Poiseuille's law — resistance depends overwhelmingly on radius: R ∝ 1 / r⁴. So halving the radius increases resistance 16-fold — tiny changes in arteriolar calibre produce huge changes in flow/BP.
  • This is why arterioles control everything: a small amount of smooth-muscle constriction dramatically raises resistance — the physical basis of all vasoconstrictor/vasodilator effects (and why arterioles, not capillaries, are the control point)
  • Resistance also rises with blood viscosity (e.g. polycythaemia) and vessel length (fixed) — but radius dominates
Pressure Across the Circulation
  • High + pulsatile in arteries (systolic/diastolic)
  • The steepest drop is across the arterioles (highest resistance) → this dampens the pulsatility
  • Low + steady in capillaries (protects the fragile exchange vessels) and veins
Mean arterial pressure (MAP) = the average arterial pressure driving organ perfusion: MAP ≈ diastolic + ⅓(pulse pressure), or MAP = CO × SVR. Pulse pressure = systolic − diastolic; widened in stiff arteries (age, atherosclerosis, aortic regurgitation), narrowed in low-SV states (shock, aortic stenosis).

Overview — Coronary Circulation
The coronary circulation supplies the myocardium itself — and has unique features that make the heart especially vulnerable to ischaemia.
The two defining peculiarities: (1) the heart extracts almost all the oxygen from coronary blood at rest, so it meets increased demand only by increasing flow, not extraction; and (2) the LV is perfused during diastole, not systole (it squeezes its own vessels shut when it contracts).
Why it matters: the direct physiological basis of angina, MI, and the anti-anginal drugs — cross-ref ACS/angina, the cardiac cycle (diastole), atherosclerosis, BP regulation.

High-yield link: the RCA usually supplies the SA and AV nodes → an inferior (RCA) MI characteristically causes bradyarrhythmias/heart block. Coronary filling happens at the aortic root → aortic regurgitation/stenosis can compromise coronary perfusion.
The Two Defining Physiological Features
Feature 1 — High oxygen extraction at rest
  • The myocardium extracts ~70–80% of oxygen from coronary blood even at rest (most tissues ~25%)
  • Little "extraction reserve" → to meet increased demand the heart must increase coronary blood flow
  • Achieved by metabolic vasodilation (local metabolites, esp. adenosine, dilate coronary arterioles when O₂ demand rises) — coronary autoregulation / metabolic hyperaemia
Clinical payoff: if a coronary artery is stenosed, flow can't rise enough to meet increased demand → demand outstrips supply → angina (pain on exertion, relieved by rest).
Feature 2 — Diastolic perfusion of the LV
  • During systole, the contracting LV compresses its own intramural vessels → LV coronary flow is squeezed off
  • So the LV is perfused mainly during diastole (muscle relaxes, vessels open)
  • Tachycardia is dangerous in ischaemia: ↑HR shortens diastole disproportionately → less coronary filling time and ↑O₂ demand (a double hit — why β-blockers help angina)
  • Coronary perfusion pressure = aortic diastolic − LV end-diastolic pressure → adequate diastolic BP matters
  • The subendocardium (innermost LV) is most vulnerable to ischaemia (furthest from epicardial vessels, highest wall stress) — first to infarct
Myocardial Oxygen Supply vs Demand — the unifying framework
Ischaemia = demand exceeding supply — every anti-anginal drug works by tipping this balance:
Side Determinants How to improve it

DemandHeart rate, contractility, afterload (wall tension), preloadβ-blockers (↓HR/contractility), CCB (↓afterload/HR), nitrates (↓preload)
Anti-anginal logic: β-blockers ↓HR (↓demand + ↑diastolic filling); nitrates ↓preload + dilate coronaries (↓demand + ↑supply); CCBs ↓afterload/HR — all tip the supply-demand balance back.
When Supply Fails: Ischaemia → Infarction
  • Stable angina: fixed stenosis → demand-led ischaemia (exertion) → reversible, relieved by rest/GTN
  • Acute coronary syndrome: plaque rupture → thrombus → acute supply failure → unstable angina/NSTEMI (partial) or STEMI (complete occlusion → transmural infarct) — cross-ref ACS
  • The territories map to the ECG leads (anterior/lateral/inferior — above)
  • Collateral circulation: gradual stenosis can stimulate collaterals (partial protection); sudden occlusion gives no time for this → why acute occlusion is so damaging

Overview
Stable Angina
Chest pain/discomfort from myocardial ischaemia caused by demand > supply across a fixed atheromatous plaque. Stable = predictable, exertional, relieves with rest/GTN. Part of the stable CAD → ACS spectrum.

Angina Classification — 3-Feature Typicality Ladder

Category Criteria Features present
Typical angina All 3 features Constricting central/retrosternal pain ± radiation AND brought on by exertion/stress AND relieved by rest or GTN within ~5 min
Atypical angina 2 of 3 features Two of the above three characteristics
Non-anginal chest pain ≤1 of 3 features One or none of the above — unlikely cardiac ischaemia
Unstable angina → ACS pathway Pain at rest / rapidly worsening / new onset within 2 weeks — see ACS tabs
Pathophysiology
Endothelial dysfunction → LDL infiltration → foam cells → fibrous plaque → fixed flow-limiting stenosis → exertional demand exceeds supply → subendocardial ischaemia → angina. Plaque is stable — no rupture.
Stable angina: fixed stenosis → ischaemia only when demand ↑ (exertion, emotion, cold). Plaque intact. Predictable symptoms.
ACS (acute end): plaque ruptures → thrombus → partial or complete coronary occlusion → ischaemia at rest. Unpredictable.
Investigations

Bloods

  • FBC (anaemia aggravates ischaemia), U&E, lipids, HbA1c
  • LFTs before starting a statin (baseline)
  • TFTs (thyroid disease can worsen angina)
  • Troponin only if unstable/acute presentation — not routine in stable angina

Resting ECG

  • Often normal between episodes
  • May show old Q waves (previous MI), ST depression, T-wave changes
  • Performed in all patients; helps exclude other diagnoses

CT Coronary Angiography (CTCA) — First-Line (NICE)

Non-invasive imaging of coronary arteries. NICE recommends CTCA as the first-line investigation for stable chest pain of suspected cardiac origin with no known CAD. Identifies plaque burden, degree of stenosis, and non-obstructive disease. Excellent negative predictive value — rules out significant CAD effectively.

Functional Imaging

  • Stress echocardiography — exercise or dobutamine; wall motion abnormalities
  • Stress cardiac MRI — perfusion imaging with adenosine
  • Myocardial perfusion imaging (MPI) — nuclear; identifies ischaemic territory
  • Used if CTCA non-diagnostic or to assess functional significance of stenosis

Invasive Coronary Angiography

  • Gold standard for coronary anatomy and severity
  • Allows simultaneous PCI (angioplasty + stent)
  • Indicated when CTCA/functional imaging shows significant disease or revascularisation planned
  • FFR (fractional flow reserve) guides intervention decision

Three things always happening simultaneously — this is how the examiners test it:

Arm 1 — Secondary Prevention (modify risk / prevent MI)

  • Aspirin 75 mg OD — indefinitely; single antiplatelet only (cf. DAPT in ACS)
  • Clopidogrel 75 mg OD if aspirin intolerant

  • Atorvastatin 80 mg ON — high-intensity; ↓ LDL → plaque stabilisation
  • Check LFTs at baseline and at 3 months

  • If co-existing diabetes, hypertension, CKD, or HF
  • Cardioprotective; ↓ afterload and vascular tone

  • Smoking cessation (most important)
  • BP control (target <130/80)
  • Glycaemic control in diabetes
  • Weight, exercise, diet

  • Mechanism: NO donor → venodilation → ↓ preload → ↓ myocardial oxygen demand; also dilates coronary arteries
  • Protocol: 1 dose → wait 5 min → 2nd dose → wait 5 min → call 999 if no relief (possible ACS)
  • Can use before anticipated exertion (prophylactic)
  • Side effect: headache (vasodilation), flushing, hypotension
  • Store away from light/heat; expires 8 weeks after opening (spray lasts longer)

↓ wait 5 min

↓ wait 5 min

  • Never BB + verapamil/diltiazem → risk of heart block

  • Long-acting nitrate (ISMN — isosorbide mononitrate)
  • Ivabradine (If-channel; HR-lowering; if BB intolerant, sinus rhythm only)
  • Nicorandil (K-ATP opener + nitrate)
  • Ranolazine (late Na-channel inhibitor)

Revascularisation

For significant stenosis confirmed on imaging or refractory symptoms despite optimal medical therapy:

PCI — Percutaneous Coronary Intervention

  • Coronary angioplasty + stent (drug-eluting stent preferred)
  • Suitable for single or discrete vessel disease
  • Less invasive, shorter recovery
  • DAPT required post-stent (aspirin + clopidogrel) for 1–12 months

CABG — Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting

  • Grafts: LIMA (left internal mammary artery) — best patency; saphenous vein; radial artery
  • Favoured over PCI in: left main stem disease, severe/multivessel disease, diabetes mellitus, poor LV function (EF <30%)
  • Better long-term outcomes in complex disease
LIMA graft (left internal mammary → LAD) has >90% patency at 10 years — the gold standard bypass graft. Saphenous vein grafts: ~50% patency at 10 years.

Never BB + verapamil/diltiazem → sinus arrest / complete heart block. BB + amlodipine is safe.

Definition & Classification

A clinical syndrome resulting from structural or functional cardiac abnormality → inability to maintain adequate cardiac output at normal filling pressures.

  • Valvular disease (aortic stenosis is common)
  • Arrhythmias (AF is common)

  • Thyrotoxicosis
  • Paget's disease of bone
  • Pregnancy
  • Beriberi (thiamine deficiency)

Modern practice favours early initiation of all four pillars together (or in rapid sequence) rather than strict sequential step-up — current ESC/NICE guidance.

② Beta-blocker
Bisoprolol / carvedilol / nebivolol only. Blocks chronically activated SNS → ↓HR, anti-remodelling. NOT atenolol/metoprolol. Start low, titrate slow.
③ MRA
Spironolactone / eplerenone. Blocks aldosterone → ↓fibrosis + ↓K⁺ loss. Hyperkalaemia risk — monitor K⁺ + renal function.
④ SGLT2i

CARDIOVASCULAR__Acute Heart Failure:
Definition & Mechanism

Acute Heart Failure (AHF) occurs when an acute event renders the LV unable to efficiently pump blood into the systemic circulation → backlog in LA, pulmonary veins, and lungs → pulmonary oedema (lung tissue and alveoli filled with interstitial fluid).

De Novo AHF
First-ever presentation — no prior HF diagnosis. Often caused by new MI, hypertensive emergency, or acute valve rupture. Requires full diagnostic workup.
Decompensated Chronic HF
Known HF, acutely worsened by a trigger. More common. Identify and treat the trigger while optimising chronic therapy.
Decompensation Triggers

AHF is often decompensated chronic HF precipitated by one of these triggers:

MI / ACS New AF / arrhythmia Hypertensive emergency Sepsis / infection Iatrogenic IV fluids Non-compliance with meds Anaemia / PE Valvular rupture
Clinical Features

Symptoms

  • Acute SOB — worse lying flat, improves sitting up
  • Cough with frothy white/pink sputum
  • Raised RR, reduced O₂ sats
  • Extreme anxiety / sense of impending doom

Signs

  • Tachycardia, tachypnoea
  • 3rd heart sound
  • Bilateral basal crackles
  • Hypotension in severe cases (cardiogenic shock)
  • Signs of underlying cause: chest pain (ACS), fever (sepsis), palpitations (arrhythmia)
  • If R-sided HF too: raised JVP, peripheral oedema

Look for arrhythmias (AF), ischaemia (STEMI/NSTEMI), LBBB — identifies the trigger

Assess degree of hypoxia and hypercapnia; guides need for NIV/intubation
🩻

Alveolar oedema · Kerley B lines · Cardiomegaly · Upper lobe diversion · Pleural effusion
📊

Assess LV function and structural abnormalities — identifies cause (e.g. valve rupture, wall motion abnormality)

Requires hospital admission. Severe pulmonary oedema / cardiogenic shock → HDU or ITU.

CARDIOVASCULAR__Hypertension:
Definition & Staging

Sustained elevation of BP — the "silent killer" — usually asymptomatic until end-organ damage occurs. Diagnosed via clinic measurement then confirmed with ABPM or HBPM (ambulatory/home) to exclude white-coat effect.

StageClinic BPABPM / HBPMAction
Stage 1≥140/90≥135/85Treat if <80 yrs with end-organ damage, CV risk >10%, or T2DM/CKD
Stage 2≥160/100≥150/95Offer treatment regardless of other factors
Stage 3 / Severe≥180/120—Same-day assessment for end-organ damage; if present → hypertensive emergency
Key diagnostic rule: Clinic BP 140/90–180/120 → confirm with ABPM or HBPM before diagnosing. Treat to the lower ambulatory threshold. White-coat hypertension is common — ABPM prevents over-treatment.
Aetiology
Primary / Essential — 90%
  • No identifiable cause
  • Polygenic — multiple genes + lifestyle
  • Risk factors: age, obesity, high salt diet, alcohol, sedentary lifestyle, smoking, family history
  • Mechanism: ↑RAAS activity, sympathetic overdrive, impaired renal sodium excretion
Secondary — 10%
  • Renal (commonest ~80% of secondary): CKD, renovascular disease (RAS — especially if treatment-resistant), polycystic kidney disease
  • Endocrine: Conn's syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism), phaeochromocytoma, Cushing's, acromegaly, hypothyroidism
  • Other: Coarctation of the aorta (young patients), pre-eclampsia, OSA
  • Drugs: NSAIDs, oestrogen (OCP), alcohol, liquorice, cocaine, ciclosporin
Think secondary if: Young · Resistant (≥3 drugs) · Sudden onset — especially in patients under 40, those with refractory HTN, or an identifiable clinical clue (e.g. hypokalaemia → Conn's; episodic headache/sweating/palpitations → phaeochromocytoma).
Clinical Features & Secondary-Cause Clues

Primary hypertension is largely asymptomatic. Symptoms usually signify end-organ damage or an underlying secondary cause.

Drug choice is driven by age and ethnicity because these predict renin status — the mechanism that determines which drug class works best.

Renin logic (makes it memorable): Younger/Caucasian = high-renin → RAAS-dependent → ACEi/ARB works. Older/Black African/Caribbean = low-renin → volume-dependent → CCB or diuretic works.

Malignant / accelerated HTN = BP ≥180/120 + evidence of end-organ damage. Severity is defined by damage, not the number alone.

Lower BP slowly — rapid reduction causes cerebral and renal hypoperfusion. Aim to reduce MAP by no more than 25% in the first hour, then cautiously to 160/100 over 2–6 hours.

  • GTN infusion — ACS/acute LVF component

  • Same-day referral to specialist centre

  • ECG — LVH, ischaemia
  • CXR — pulmonary oedema, widened mediastinum (dissection)
  • CT head if neurological symptoms

Untreated hypertension causes progressive end-organ damage — the "why we treat" framework:

🫀

🫁

👁️

🩸

Permanent localised dilatation of the abdominal aorta >3 cm (normal ~2 cm). Most are infrarenal. The vast majority are asymptomatic — found on screening or incidentally.

Two Exam Anchors

CARDIOVASCULAR__Aortic Dissection:
Overview

Aortic dissection: tear in the aortic intima → blood forces its way between intima and media → creates a false lumen that propagates along the aortic wall.

🚨 Time-Critical Emergency
  • Type A mortality rises ~1–2%/hour without surgery
  • Everything hinges on Stanford A vs B — this determines management
  • Acute = <14 days; chronic = >14 days
Propagation Direction
  • Anterograde → iliac arteries → limb ischaemia, renal/mesenteric malperfusion
  • Retrograde → aortic root → aortic regurgitation, coronary involvement, cardiac tamponade
🔗 Link to AAA/TAA: a "dissecting aneurysm" refers to an aneurysm complicated by dissection — the same connective-tissue thread (Marfan, bicuspid AV) runs through all three aortic pathologies.

CARDIOVASCULAR__Bradycardias / Heart Blo:
Definition & Organising Principle

Bradycardia = HR <60 bpm. The distinction that matters clinically is symptomatic vs incidental — symptomatic bradycardia causes haemodynamic compromise (shock, syncope, ischaemia, heart failure) and needs treatment; incidental bradycardia in an athlete or during sleep is physiologically normal.

The organising principle: anatomical level of the block determines everything — escape rate, QRS width, escape reliability, response to atropine, and whether pacing is needed.

🟢
SA Node
Sinus bradycardia, sick sinus. Escape ~60 bpm. QRS narrow. Atropine works.
🟡
AV Node
1st degree, Mobitz I. Junctional escape 40–60 bpm. QRS narrow. Usually benign. Atropine works.
🔴
Infranodal (His-Purkinje)
Mobitz II, CHB broad escape. Ventricular escape <40 bpm. QRS broad. Atropine INEFFECTIVE — must pace.
Key principle: The lower the block, the slower and broader the escape rhythm and the less reliable it is. An infranodal block cannot be treated with atropine — the drug acts on the AV node, not below it.
Sinus Bradycardia — Causes

Definition: HR <60 bpm with P waves of normal morphology preceding every QRS — the SA node fires, just slowly. Resting bradycardia is expected in athletes (enhanced vagal tone) and during sleep — no treatment needed.

Extrinsic Causes (outside the heart)
Drugs
  • β-blockers
  • Digoxin
  • Rate-limiting CCBs — verapamil, diltiazem
  • Amiodarone, lithium
Systemic
  • Hypothyroidism (myxoedema)
  • Hypothermia
  • ↑ICP — Cushing's reflex (bradycardia + hypertension + irregular respirations)
  • Cholestasis — bile salts vagotonic on SA node
Intrinsic Causes (within the heart)
  • Acute ischaemia / inferior MI — RCA supplies SA node in 60%; vagally mediated
  • Sick sinus syndrome — see below
Sick Sinus Syndrome (SSS)
Sick Sinus Syndrome = SA node dysfunction encompassing several patterns: idiopathic degenerative fibrosis (commonest; elderly), persistent symptomatic sinus bradycardia, prolonged pauses (SA exit block / sinus arrest), and brady-tachy syndrome — alternating bradycardia and paroxysmal AF/flutter. Treating the tachy can worsen the brady.
Brady-Tachy Syndrome
  • Alternating sinus bradycardia and paroxysmal AF or flutter
  • Antiarrhythmics to treat AF worsen bradycardia
  • Pacemaker first — then safe to use antiarrhythmics
  • Anticoagulation for AF component
Management
  • Treat reversible cause: stop offending drugs, replace thyroid hormone
  • Atropine for acute symptomatic episodes
  • Permanent pacemaker if symptomatic and cause not reversible
AV Block Classification

AV blocks are a spectrum of worsening AV conduction. The key discriminator is not just the degree but where in the conduction system the block sits — nodal vs infranodal.

1°
1st Degree
PR >200ms, fixed. Every P conducts. AV node. Benign — no treatment.
2°A
Mobitz I — Wenckebach
Progressive PR lengthening → dropped QRS → resets. AV node. Narrow QRS. Usually benign.
2°B
Mobitz II
Fixed PR → sudden dropped QRS. INFRANODAL. Broad QRS. HIGH risk of CHB → pacemaker.
3°
Complete Heart Block
P waves and QRS fully dissociated. Escape rhythm only. Wide QRS = infranodal (unreliable). Pacemaker mandatory.

Complete Heart Block — Escape Rhythm Comparison

In CHB, ventricular output depends entirely on a spontaneous escape rhythm below the block. The level determines reliability.

Narrow Escape (His Bundle)
  • Rate: 50–60 bpm
  • QRS: narrow (<120ms)
  • Reliable pacemaker
  • Often inferior MI / reversible cause
  • May respond to IV atropine acutely
  • Still usually needs permanent pacing
Broad Escape (His-Purkinje)
  • Rate: <40 bpm
  • QRS: broad (>120ms)
  • Unreliable — may fail without warning
  • Causes Stokes-Adams attacks
  • Atropine INEFFECTIVE
  • Permanent pacemaker mandatory
Stokes-Adams attacks: Sudden LOC from CHB → transient asystole or VT → rapid complete recovery without post-ictal confusion. Pale then flushed as circulation restores. No tongue-biting, no incontinence. Distinguish from epilepsy by the rapid complete return to normal.
Bundle Branch Block — LBBB & RBBB

BBB is a conduction delay, not a bradycardia. Covered here as part of the conduction system. The AV node and His bundle conduct normally — the delay is in one bundle branch → wide QRS (>120ms) with characteristic morphology.

LBBB — WiLLiaM
  • W in V1 — deep QS or rS wave
  • M in V5/V6 and I — broad notched R wave
  • QRS >120ms · Left axis deviation
  • Always pathological — AS, HTN, IHD, cardiomyopathy
  • New LBBB + chest pain = STEMI equivalent → PPCI
RBBB — MaRRoW
  • M in V1 — RSR' pattern ('rabbit ears')
  • W in V5/V6 and I — broad slurred S wave
  • QRS >120ms · Right axis deviation
  • Can be normal variant in young people
  • Also: PE (acute RV strain), RVH, congenital HD

CARDIOVASCULAR__Cardiac Arrest / Advance:
The Four Arrest Rhythms
Rhythm classification determines the entire management pathway. Shock the non-shockable and you waste time; delay adrenaline in non-shockable and you lose the only treatment that works.
⚡ Shockable
Ventricular Fibrillation (VF)
Chaotic, disorganised electrical activity — ventricles quivering with no coordinated contraction. ECG shows erratic fibrillatory waveforms with no discernible QRS complexes.
Pulseless VT (pVT)
Organised ventricular tachycardia (wide QRS, rate >100) but with no palpable pulse — too fast for effective cardiac output.
Why shock works: A single high-energy shock simultaneously depolarises the entire myocardium → brief asystole → intrinsic pacemakers can restart a coordinated rhythm.
🚫 Non-Shockable
Pulseless Electrical Activity (PEA)
Organised electrical activity on the monitor (looks like a rhythm) but no palpable pulse. The heart’s electrical system is intact but mechanical function has failed. Almost always caused by a reversible 4H/4T.
Asystole
Flat line — no electrical activity. Terminal unless an underlying cause is identified and reversed rapidly.
Why no shock: There is no disorganised electrical activity to “reset.” Defibrillating PEA or asystole does not help and wastes critical time.

Reversible Causes — 4Hs & 4Ts
Non-shockable rhythms are won by finding and fixing the reversible cause. Drugs alone will not restart the heart. In shockable rhythms, always search simultaneously — failure to find the cause leads to re-arrest after ROSC.
The 4 Hs
💨 Hypoxia
Recognise: Low SpO₂, cyanosis, poor bag-mask seal, obstructed airway, inadequate ventilation
Treat: Ensure airway open and patent · High-flow O₂ · Confirm ETT position · Suction
💉 Hypovolaemia
Recognise: Visible haemorrhage, trauma, flat neck veins, haematemesis, AAA
Treat: Rapid IV/IO fluids · Blood products early · Control haemorrhage source (surgery/IR if needed)
⚖️ Hypo/Hyperkalaemia & Metabolic
Recognise: Known renal failure, peaked T / broad QRS / sine wave (hyperkalaemia), diabetic patient (hypo K/glucose/Ca)
Treat: Calcium chloride 10% 10mL IV (hyperkalaemia) · 50% dextrose (hypoglycaemia) · Magnesium (hypoMg) · Sodium bicarbonate if severe acidosis or TCA overdose
❄️ Hypothermia
Recognise: Cold patient, core temp <30°C, J-waves (Osborn waves) on ECG, drowning/exposure
Treat: Warm IV fluids · External warming (warm blankets, warmed humidified O₂) · ECMO for deep hypothermia
Rule: “Not dead until warm and dead” — do not stop CPR until core temp >35°C
The 4 Ts
❤️ Thrombosis — Coronary
Recognise: Preceding chest pain, STEMI on ECG, known CAD
Treat: CPR whilst arranging → PCI (primary PPCI) post-ROSC · Thrombolysis if PCI unavailable and PE also suspected
🫀 Thrombosis — Pulmonary (PE)
Recognise: PE risk factors, RBBB pattern, no other cause found, sudden arrest
Treat: Thrombolysis (alteplase 50mg IV) — continue CPR for 60–90 min after · Surgical embolectomy if available
🪵 Tension Pneumothorax
Recognise: Unequal/absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation (late), traumatic arrest, ventilated patient
Treat: Immediate needle decompression → 2nd ICS midclavicular line → confirm with finger thoracostomy → chest drain
🫀 Tamponade — Cardiac
Recognise: Penetrating chest trauma, known pericardial disease, Beck’s triad (JVP↑, hypotension, muffled HS), POCUS (pericardial effusion)
Treat: Pericardiocentesis (US-guided) · Emergency thoracotomy if traumatic arrest
☢️ Toxins
Recognise: Known ingestion/exposure, bradyarrhythmia or tachyarrhythmia, miosis/mydriasis, history
Treat: Specific antidote if available: atropine (organophosphates) · naloxone (opioids) · lipid emulsion 20% (local anaesthetic toxicity) · digoxin-specific antibody fragments (digoxin) · activated charcoal only if alert and within 1 hour
POCUS during arrest: Cardiac motion? (fine VF vs. true asystole) · Pericardial effusion? · IVC flat? (hypovolaemia) · Pleural fluid? · Requires <10 sec at pulse check.
Defibrillation · Post-ROSC · Exam Pearls
A — Defibrillation Detail
⚡ Unsynchronised (Defibrillation)
  • Use for: VF / pulseless VT
  • No organised R waves to synchronise to → device delivers shock immediately on button press
  • Energy: 120–150J biphasic (first shock); escalate for subsequent shocks up to device maximum
  • Pad placement: right infraclavicular + left lateral (V5 position) or anterior-posterior
📶 Synchronised (Cardioversion)
  • Use for: Organised tachyarrhythmia WITH a pulse
  • Device waits for R wave, then shocks → avoids delivering shock during vulnerable T-wave period (R-on-T → VF)
  • See Tachycardia notes §4/§5 for unstable tachycardia management
  • Energy: 70–120J biphasic (AF); 50–100J (flutter/SVT)
Defibrillation safety drill: “Stand clear · Oxygen away (≥1 m from patient) · All clear · Shock” — Visually confirm all personnel clear before each shock.
B — Post-ROSC Care
Immediate (minutes)
  • ABCDE reassessment
  • SpO₂ 94–98% (avoid hyperoxia)
  • Aim normocapnia (PaCO₂ 4.5–6.0 kPa)
  • IV fluid if hypotensive · vasopressors if needed
  • 12-lead ECG: STEMI? → emergency PCI (see ACS notes)
Ongoing (ICU)
  • Targeted temperature management: Prevent fever (target 36°C); consider cooling to 33°C for comatose survivors
  • Identify and treat cause (4Hs/4Ts, CTPA, echo, coronary angiography)
  • Neuroprotection · seizure monitoring · glucose control
  • Prognostication: not before 72h (hypothermia delays neurological assessment)
C — DNACPR & When to Stop
  • DNACPR order: Valid order in place → do not start CPR. Must be clearly documented and accessible.
  • Do not start CPR if: Valid DNACPR · Injuries incompatible with life · Rigor mortis / dependent lividity present
  • Stop CPR if: ROSC achieved · All reversible causes excluded · Prolonged ALS without ROSC (>20–30 min in most cases) · Team leader consensus
  • Hypothermic arrest exception: Continue until core temperature >35°C or ECMO available — “not dead until warm and dead”
⭐ Exam Pearls
Adrenaline timing trap: Non-shockable → give adrenaline immediately. Shockable → give adrenaline only after the 3rd shock (not the 1st). This is the most-tested ALS fact.
Amiodarone is ONLY for the shockable arm. Never give amiodarone in PEA or asystole — it has no role and no evidence.
Magnesium 2g IV is the specific treatment for torsades de pointes (polymorphic VT / long QT) — see Irregular Broad tab in Tachycardia notes. Magnesium is NOT routine in all cardiac arrests.
Non-shockable rhythms are won by the 4Hs & 4Ts. No drug can restart a heart that has failed due to tamponade, tension pneumo, or massive PE — fix the cause.
Monitored arrest: 3 stacked shocks first (without CPR between), then begin the standard ALS cycle — only applies when the defibrillator is immediately available and arrest is witnessed.
Post-ROSC 12-lead ECG: STEMI after ROSC → emergency PCI. This is the most time-critical post-arrest intervention (see ACS notes).
CARDIOVASCULAR__Myocarditis:
Definition & The Core Concept

Myocarditis = inflammation of the myocardium → myocyte damage, ventricular dysfunction, and arrhythmia.

Typical course: a viral prodrome (fever, fatigue, myalgia) → days to weeks later → cardiac symptoms (chest pain, dyspnoea, palpitations, heart failure).
Key clinical flag: a young patient + chest pain + recent viral illness → think myocarditis before ACS. Troponin raised but coronaries normal.
Aetiology
🦠 Viral — commonest in the UK
  • Coxsackie B — most common overall
  • Adenovirus, parvovirus B19, CMV, EBV
  • HIV (direct infection + immunosuppression)
  • Influenza, SARS-CoV-2
🧫 Bacterial, spirochaete & protozoal
  • Bacteria: diphtheria (toxin-mediated), Clostridia
  • Spirochaete: Lyme disease (Borrelia)
  • Protozoa: Chagas' disease (Trypanosoma cruzi), toxoplasmosis
💊 Drugs & toxins
  • Doxorubicin (dose-dependent cardiotoxicity)
  • Immune checkpoint inhibitors (pembrolizumab, nivolumab — high-yield emerging cause)
  • Cocaine, alcohol, radiation, clozapine
🛡️ Autoimmune & infiltrative
  • SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, sarcoidosis
  • Giant cell myocarditis (rare, aggressive)
  • Eosinophilic myocarditis (drug hypersensitivity)
Clinical Features

Symptoms arise from two overlapping processes — the inflammatory process itself and secondary myocardial dysfunction (heart failure):

🔥 Inflammatory symptoms
  • Recent viral prodrome: fever, rash, GI upset, myalgia, arthralgia
  • Chest pain — sharp/stabbing, may be pleuritic
  • Dizziness, syncope (arrhythmia)
  • Can overlap with pericarditis → myopericarditis
💔 Heart failure / muscle dysfunction
  • Dyspnoea on exertion → orthopnoea
  • Fatigue, ankle oedema
  • Biventricular failure (acute dilated picture)
  • Palpitations (VT, VF risk)
🩺 Signs on examination
  • Tachycardia (often disproportionate)
  • Soft/muffled heart sounds
  • S3 gallop (ventricular dysfunction)S3 gallop — Judge & Mangrulkar, University of Michigan Heart Sound & Murmur Library, CC BY-SA 3.0.
  • Bibasal crackles (left heart failure)
  • ↑JVP, oedema (right heart failure)
  • Hypotension (fulminant)
  • Fever, signs of viral illness
  • Pericardial rub (myopericarditis)
Investigations
🩸 Bloods
  • ↑Troponin / CK-MB — myocyte damage (mimics ACS)
  • ↑BNP / NT-proBNP — ventricular dysfunction
  • ↑ESR, CRP, WBC — inflammation
  • Viral serology (paired titres), autoimmune screen
📈 ECG
  • Diffuse non-specific ST/T changes — key difference from STEMI (territory-based)
  • Sinus tachycardia, heart block, VT/AF
  • Can mimic STEMI: widespread ST elevation
  • Serial ECGs important
🫀 Echocardiography
  • Ventricular dilatation, ↓EF, wall-motion abnormalities
  • Pericardial effusion if myopericarditis
  • Excludes structural/valve pathology
🩻 Chest X-ray
  • Cardiomegaly (significant LV dilatation)
  • Pulmonary oedema / pleural effusions if heart failure
  • May be normal in early/mild disease
⭐ Cardiac MRI — key modern test
  • Non-invasive gold standard in clinical practice
  • Late gadolinium enhancement → myocardial inflammation/fibrosis
  • Lake Louise criteria for diagnosis
  • Guides prognosis + risk stratification
🔬 Endomyocardial biopsy
  • Pathological gold standard — Dallas criteria; rarely done (risk vs benefit)
  • Reserved for: haemodynamic compromise, suspected giant cell / eosinophilic, unclear diagnosis after non-invasive workup
  • Histology: inflammatory infiltrate (lymphocytes/neutrophils) + myocyte necrosis; identifies aetiology (viral, giant cell, eosinophilic)
Management

Supportive care is the mainstay — most cases are self-limiting. Treat the underlying cause where possible.

🛟 Supportive measures
  • Hospital admission + cardiac monitoring (arrhythmia risk)
  • Bed rest
  • Treat heart failure: diuretics, ACEi/ARB, beta-blockers (once stable)
  • Anti-arrhythmics if needed; defibrillator on standby
  • IABP or LVAD in fulminant / cardiogenic shock
🎯 Treat the underlying cause
  • Bacterial: IV antibiotics; Lyme: doxycycline / ceftriaxone
  • Chagas': benznidazole
  • Drug-induced: stop the offending agent immediately
  • Autoimmune: steroids / immunosuppression
  • Checkpoint-inhibitor-associated: high-dose steroids, hold the inhibitor
Avoid strenuous exercise: risk of haemodynamic deterioration + life-threatening arrhythmia → abstain from competitive sport for a minimum of 3–6 months (or until MRI/echo confirms resolution). A common cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes.
✅ Good prognosis (majority)
  • Most viral myocarditis resolves spontaneously
  • Full recovery of cardiac function in weeks–months
  • Viral cause with mild dysfunction: excellent outlook
Poor prognostic factors
  • Fulminant presentation / cardiogenic shock
  • Giant cell myocarditis (aggressive, high mortality)
  • Progression to dilated cardiomyopathy
  • Sudden cardiac death (young athletes, arrhythmia)
  • Persistent LV dysfunction at 6 months → transplant consideration
Exam Pearls
Think myocarditis
Young patient + chest pain + recent viral illness → troponin raised but coronaries normal on angiography.
Commonest cause
UK = Coxsackie B; South America = Chagas' disease (Trypanosoma cruzi).
Diagnosis
Cardiac MRI = key non-invasive test (late gadolinium enhancement); endomyocardial biopsy = pathological gold standard (rarely done).
Myopericarditis
Overlap with pericarditis → pericardial rub + troponin rise + ST changes — treat both components.
Checkpoint inhibitors
Immune checkpoint inhibitors (pembrolizumab, nivolumab) → fulminant myocarditis — stop the drug + high-dose steroids urgently.
Complications
Important cause of dilated cardiomyopathy + sudden cardiac death in young people — avoid exercise for ≥3–6 months.
CARDIOVASCULAR__Lipid Disorders / Athero:
Overview

Atherosclerosis: chronic arterial wall inflammation → lipid deposition → fibrous plaque formation → arterial stiffening, stenosis, and plaque rupture → MI, stroke, peripheral arterial disease.

Primary Prevention

No prior CVD event. Goal: calculate risk and intervene before disease manifests.

Tool: QRISK3 (10-year stroke/MI risk). Threshold: ≥10% → atorvastatin 20mg

Secondary Prevention

Post-CVD event (MI, stroke, PVD). Goal: prevent recurrence.

Atorvastatin 80mg + the 4 A's — regardless of baseline cholesterol

⭐ The primary vs secondary fork drives everything: statin dose, antiplatelet choice, and beta-blocker use all differ between the two arms.
Risk Factors
🔒
Non-Modifiable
Age · Male sex · Family history of premature CVD
🔧
Modifiable
Raised cholesterol · Smoking · Alcohol · Poor diet · Physical inactivity · Obesity · Poor sleep · Stress
🩺
Comorbidities
Diabetes · Hypertension · CKD · Inflammatory disease (RA, SLE) · Atypical antipsychotics (↑metabolic risk)
Clinical Features
Hyperlipidaemia is usually asymptomatic — picked up on routine bloods or screening. Signs below indicate severe / longstanding disease.
🤜
Tendon Xanthomata
Hard nodules of cholesterol deposition. Sites: knuckles (extensor tendons), Achilles tendon. Pathognomonic of familial hypercholesterolaemia
👁️
Xanthelasma
Yellowish plaques on the eyelids. Associated with dyslipidaemia but may occur with normal lipids
🔵
Corneal Arcus
Grey-white ring at corneal periphery. Premature (<45 years) = lipid disorder; normal in elderly
🔥
Acute Pancreatitis
Severe hypertriglyceridaemia (>10 mmol/L) can precipitate acute pancreatitis — a serious complication
Lifestyle Optimisation (All Patients)
Diet
  • Total fat <30% of caloric intake
  • Saturated fat <7% of calories
  • ↓ sugar, ↓ refined carbohydrates
  • 5-a-day fruit and vegetables
  • ≥2 portions oily fish per week
  • ↓ salt (especially if hypertensive)
Exercise & Habits
  • 150 min moderate OR 75 min vigorous aerobic/week
  • + 2× strength/resistance training/week
  • Smoking cessation (single most effective CVD intervention)
  • Alcohol: ≤14 units/week, spread across ≥3 days
  • Treat comorbidities: HTN, diabetes, obesity
Primary Prevention
Calculate QRISK3 score (10-year cardiovascular risk)
≥10% risk → offer atorvastatin 20 mg nocte after lifestyle discussion
Recheck lipids at 3 months — aim ≥40% reduction in non-HDL cholesterol
Automatic Statin (No QRISK Required)
CKD (eGFR <60 or ACR ≥3)
  • Atorvastatin 20 mg regardless of QRISK
  • CKD independently multiplies CVD risk
Type 1 Diabetes
  • Atorvastatin 20 mg if: >40 years, OR diabetes >10 years, OR nephropathy
  • No QRISK calculation needed
Secondary Prevention — The 4 A's
⭐ After any CVD event (MI, stroke, TIA, PVD): start atorvastatin 80 mg + the 4 A's — regardless of baseline cholesterol level.
A
Atorvastatin 80 mg
High-intensity statin nocte. Target ≥40% ↓ non-HDL. Note: 20 mg in primary prevention
A
Antiplatelet
Aspirin 75 mg OD (indefinite) · Post-MI: DAPT = aspirin + clopidogrel/ticagrelor for 12 months
A
Atenolol / Beta-Blocker
Bisoprolol or atenolol — rate control, reduce cardiac remodelling post-MI, reduce sudden death risk
A
ACE Inhibitor
Ramipril / perindopril — BP control, cardioprotection, remodelling prevention post-MI
🔑 Key contrast: Primary = atorvastatin 20 mg alone (if QRISK ≥10%); Secondary = atorvastatin 80 mg + antiplatelet + beta-blocker + ACEi
Statins — Mechanism, Monitoring & Safety
Mechanism

Inhibit HMG-CoA reductase → ↓ hepatic cholesterol synthesis → upregulate LDL receptors → ↓ LDL · Taken at night (hepatic cholesterol synthesis peaks nocturnally)

Monitoring
TimeWhat to CheckAction
Baseline Fasting lipids, LFTs, CK, TFTs, HbA1c Establish baseline before starting
3 months Fasting lipids + LFTs Aim ≥40% ↓ non-HDL. If ALT/AST >3× ULN → stop statin
12 months LFTs Mild transaminase rise acceptable; >3× ULN → stop
If muscle pain CK CK >5× ULN = rhabdomyolysis → stop immediately
Side Effects & Interactions
💪
Myopathy → Rhabdomyolysis
Muscle pain/weakness → check CK. CK >5× ULN = rhabdomyolysis → stop statin. Dark urine (myoglobinuria) = emergency
🩸
↑ T2DM Risk
Modest increase in diabetes risk — benefit vs CVD risk still strongly favours statins in most patients
🧠
Haemorrhagic Stroke
Small increased risk — relevant consideration in patients with prior haemorrhagic stroke
💊
Clarithromycin Interaction
Hold statin while on macrolide antibiotics (clarithromycin, erythromycin) — CYP3A4 inhibition → ↑ statin levels → ↑ myopathy risk
Other Lipid-Lowering Agents
🛑
Ezetimibe
Blocks intestinal cholesterol absorption (NPC1L1 inhibitor). Used as add-on to statin or in statin-intolerant patients. Well tolerated
💉
PCSK9 Inhibitors
Evolocumab, alirocumab — monoclonal antibodies, subcut every 2–4 weeks. Prevent LDL receptor degradation → profound LDL reduction. For FH or refractory hypercholesterolaemia
🐟
Omega-3 / Fibrates
Fibrates (fenofibrate) — for severe hypertriglyceridaemia. Omega-3 fatty acids — adjunct for triglyceride lowering
Familial Hypercholesterolaemia (FH)
Key Features
  • Autosomal dominant — LDL receptor mutation (or ApoB/PCSK9 variants)
  • Very high cholesterol from birth — dramatically accelerates atherosclerosis
  • Untreated: MI in 4th–5th decade
Diagnostic Criteria
Simon Broome Criteria
  • Total cholesterol >7.5 mmol/L (or LDL >4.9)
  • Tendon xanthomata in patient or first-degree relative
  • FHx premature CVD (MI <60 in 1st-degree, <50 in 2nd-degree relative)
  • DNA mutation in LDL receptor/ApoB/PCSK9 = definite diagnosis
Management
  • Urgent specialist referral
  • Genetic testing
  • High-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80 mg)
  • Add ezetimibe if target not met
  • PCSK9 inhibitor for refractory cases
  • Cascade screening — test all first-degree relatives
⭐ Exam Pearls
Primary prevention = atorvastatin 20 mg (QRISK ≥10%); Secondary prevention = atorvastatin 80 mg + 4 A's
Automatic statin (no QRISK): CKD (eGFR <60) or T1DM (>40 yrs / >10 yrs duration / nephropathy)
Statin monitoring: LFTs at 3 months + 12 months; CK only if muscle pain (rhabdo = CK >5× ULN + dark urine)
Hold statin while on clarithromycin — CYP3A4 interaction raises myopathy risk
Statins taken at night — cholesterol synthesis peaks nocturnally
FH: autosomal dominant, tendon xanthomata pathognomonic, Simon Broome criteria, cascade screen all 1st-degree relatives
Xanthelasma / corneal arcus / tendon xanthomata = lipid deposition signs in the examination
Severe hypertriglyceridaemia (>10 mmol/L) → acute pancreatitis
CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericardial Effusion / T:
Definition

Pericardial effusion: Accumulation of fluid in the pericardial sac. Can result from any cause of pericarditis.
Cardiac tamponade: MEDICAL EMERGENCY — large/rapidly accumulating pericardial fluid restricts diastolic ventricular filling → markedly reduced cardiac output.

KEY PRINCIPLE: Tamponade risk depends on the RATE of accumulation as much as the volume. Slow accumulation (e.g. malignancy) → pericardium stretches → can tolerate 2L. Rapid accumulation (e.g. trauma) → 200mL can cause tamponade.
Clinical Features
Pericardial Effusion
  • Effusion obscures apex beat
  • Soft/muffled heart sounds
  • May be asymptomatic if small and slowly accumulating
Beck's Triad — Cardiac Tamponade
📉
Hypotension
Reduced stroke volume from impaired diastolic filling → low BP
⬆️
Raised JVP
Elevated venous pressure — unable to fill the heart
🔇
Muffled Heart Sounds
Fluid surrounding heart dampens cardiac sounds
Other Tamponade Features
💨
Dyspnoea
Tachypnoea and air hunger from reduced CO
💗
Tachycardia
Compensatory — sympathetic activation
❄️
Cool Peripheries
Low CO → vasoconstriction → cold, clammy extremities
📈
Kussmaul's Sign
JVP paradoxically RISES on inspiration
🩺
Pulsus Paradoxus
SBP falls >10mmHg on inspiration — key clinical sign
Pulsus paradoxus mechanism: Inspiration → ↑venous return → RV expands in rigid pericardium → compresses LV → ↓LV filling → ↓SV → ↓SBP by >10mmHg. Note: absent y descent on JVP waveform in tamponade.
Investigations
🔊
ECHO — URGENT & DIAGNOSTIC
Echo-free (dark) space around heart. Shows diastolic collapse of RA/RV. Guides pericardiocentesis.
🩺
CXR
Large globular ('water bottle') heart silhouette — in slowly accumulating effusion
📋
ECG
Low-voltage complexes · Sinus tachycardia · Electrical alternans (alternating QRS amplitude) = classic tamponade finding
🔬
Pericardiocentesis
Aspiration of fluid under ECHO guidance → fluid sent for culture, cytology, TB PCR
Management
🔊
Confirm with ECHOEmergency bedside ECHO — confirms effusion and RV/RA diastolic collapse (tamponade physiology)
↓
💉
Emergency PericardiocentesisNeedle inserted into pericardial sac under ECHO guidance — drains fluid → immediate haemodynamic improvement
↓
🔁
Recurrent EffusionPericardial window or excision of pericardial segment → fluid drains into pleural/mediastinal lymphatics
↓
🏥
Surgical DrainageIf haemopericardium (trauma/aortic dissection) — surgical exploration needed
Tamponade = cardiac arrest if not drained urgently. Pericardiocentesis is lifesaving. Most effusions resolve spontaneously without tamponade. Small effusions need only treatment of underlying cause.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Beck's Triad: Hypotension + Raised JVP + Muffled heart sounds = cardiac tamponade
Pulsus paradoxus: SBP drops >10mmHg on inspiration — use sphygmomanometer. Classic tamponade sign.
Electrical alternans on ECG (alternating QRS amplitude) = pathognomonic of cardiac tamponade
Absent y descent on JVP waveform in tamponade (heart volume fixed — venous inflow cannot increase in diastole). Constrictive pericarditis has prominent y descent.
Kussmaul's sign (JVP rises on inspiration) occurs in constrictive pericarditis but is characteristically ABSENT in tamponade — pulsus paradoxus is the key inspiratory sign in tamponade. Normal: JVP falls.
ECHO is both diagnostic AND guides pericardiocentesis. Always confirm before draining.
Tamponade: slow accumulation (e.g. cancer) — pericardium stretches → tolerates larger volumes. Acute traumatic — 200mL can be fatal.
CARDIOVASCULAR__Peripheral Arterial Dise:
Overview

PAD = atherosclerotic narrowing of the arteries supplying the limbs — the "CAD of the legs." Presents on a spectrum from stable claudication to limb-threatening emergencies.

🟡 Intermittent Claudication
Crampy pain on walking, relieved by rest · ABPI 0.5–0.9 · Fontaine II
🔴 Critical Limb Ischaemia
Rest pain + ulcers + gangrene · ABPI <0.5 · Fontaine III–IV · Urgent referral
🚨 Acute Limb Ischaemia
Sudden occlusion · 6 P's · Hours to save the limb · Emergency
⭐ The key framing: claudication patients don't lose their legs — they die of MI and stroke. PAD = systemic atherosclerosis marker. Treat the whole patient, not just the leg.
ABPI — The Unifying Investigation ⭐

Ankle-Brachial Pressure Index = ankle systolic BP ÷ brachial systolic BP. Used at every stage of PAD assessment.

ABPIInterpretationAction
>1.2 Calcified/stiff arteries — falsely high Common in diabetes, advanced age — do not rely on ABPI alone; use toe-brachial index or duplex
1.0–1.2 Normal No significant PAD
0.5–0.9 Claudication Conservative management, supervised exercise, risk factor modification
<0.5 Critical ischaemia / rest pain Urgent vascular referral — revascularisation or amputation
>0.6 Safe for compression bandaging Must check before applying venous compression — do not compress an ischaemic leg
Examination Findings
Inspection
  • Pallor · cyanosis · dependent rubor (reactive hyperaemia)
  • Muscle wasting · hair loss · dry skin
  • Poor wound healing · ulcers · gangrene
  • Scars: amputation, sternotomy, calf vein harvest (prior bypass)
Palpation
  • Weak or absent pulses — femoral, popliteal, dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial
  • Reduced skin temperature · prolonged capillary refill
  • Reduced sensation (late sign — neuropathy or ischaemia)
Special Tests
Buerger's Test
  • Elevate limb → pallor (ischaemia)
  • Hang leg down → dependent rubor (reactive hyperaemia)
  • Buerger's angle <20° = severe ischaemia (angle at which pallor appears on elevation)
Leriche Syndrome (Aortoiliac Occlusion)
  • Buttock / thigh claudication
  • Absent femoral pulses bilaterally
  • Erectile dysfunction (internal iliac involvement)
  • Classic triad — high-yield exam eponym
Intermittent Claudication (Fontaine II)
Presentation
  • Cramping pain on walking, relieved by rest within minutes
  • Predictable claudication distance that reproducibly reproduces symptoms
  • Site → level: calf = femoropopliteal · thigh = iliac · buttock = aortoiliac (Leriche)
Investigations
📊
ABPI
0.5–0.9 in claudication. Baseline and follow-up
🔊
Duplex Ultrasound
First-line imaging — identifies stenosis site and severity
🖥️
MRA / CTA
Before surgical intervention — full anatomical map of disease
Management (Conservative-Led)
Conservative (First-Line)
  • 🏃 Supervised exercise programme — 2hr/week × 3 months (first-line; improves walking distance)
  • 🚬 Smoking cessation (most important intervention)
  • Diet, weight loss, glycaemic control
Medical
  • 💊 Atorvastatin 80 mg (established CVD — secondary prevention)
  • 💊 Clopidogrel 75 mg — first-line antiplatelet (aspirin if intolerant)
  • 💊 Naftidrofuryl — vasodilator for claudication if exercise programme fails
  • Optimise BP and diabetes
Surgical (Lifestyle-Limiting Only)
  • Angioplasty ± stent — short lesions (<10 cm), aortoiliac preferred
  • Bypass / endarterectomy — long / multifocal disease (>10 cm)
  • Only if conservative + medical have failed and symptoms severely limit life
Critical Limb Ischaemia (Fontaine III–IV)
⭐ CLI defined by any of: rest pain >2 weeks requiring opiates · ischaemic ulceration · gangrene · ABPI <0.5
Features
😣
Rest Pain
Worse at night (loses gravity-assisted perfusion when supine) · Patient hangs foot off the bed for relief · Requires opiates
🦶
Tissue Loss
Ischaemic ulcers (punched-out, distal) and gangrene — the end-stage of untreated CLI. See §7 and §8
🫀
Limb Signs
Pale, cold, absent pulses · atrophic shiny skin · absent hair · poor capillary refill
Management
Urgent vascular referral — same-day if acute deterioration
Revascularisation — angioplasty / stent · bypass / endarterectomy · intra-arterial thrombolysis
Amputation — if limb unreconstructable or extensive necrosis / sepsis / limited life expectancy
🚨 Acute Limb Ischaemia — The Emergency
Sudden arterial occlusion threatening limb viability within hours. Paralysis + paraesthesia = irreversible ischaemia imminent — act immediately.
The 6 P's
1
Pain
Severe, sudden — worse on elevation
2
Pallor
Skin white/waxy compared to contralateral limb
3
Pulselessness
Absent distal pulses — confirm with handheld Doppler
4
Perishing Cold
Poikilothermia — limb temperature = environment
5
Paraesthesia
Numbness/tingling — early nerve ischaemia. Threatened limb
6
Paralysis
Motor loss — LATE sign of irreversible ischaemia. Urgent surgery

ECG (AF?), handheld Doppler, serum lactate, CT arteriogram
Urgent vascular referral → embolectomy / thrombolysis / angioplasty
Irreversible (mottled non-blanching skin + woody hard muscles) → amputation

⭐ Safety rule 2: X-ray any deep neuropathic ulcer for osteomyelitis (if bone is visible, osteomyelitis is confirmed).
Gangrene — End-Stage Tissue Death
Gangrene = irreversible tissue death. It is the endpoint of the ischaemia pathway (Fontaine IV / CLI's worst) — dry and wet gangrene from ischaemia; gas gangrene from infection.
⬛
Dry Gangrene
Ischaemic, aseptic · Dehydrated, mummified, black · Well-defined demarcation line · Classic PAD endpoint · Typically affects digits · Mx: revascularise where possible; allow auto-amputation or surgical amputation
🟤
Wet Gangrene
Ischaemia + infection · Moist, swollen, foul-smelling · No clear demarcation · Surgical emergency — rapid spread · Common in diabetics · Mx: urgent debridement + IV antibiotics + revascularisation
💨
Gas Gangrene 🚨
Clostridium perfringens · Post-trauma / contaminated wound · Crepitus on palpation + gas on X-ray · Extremely rapid spread · Life-threatening · Mx: emergency surgical debridement + IV penicillin / clindamycin + fasciotomies + hyperbaric O₂
Amputation — Primary Indications
  • Extensive weight-bearing necrosis
  • Uncontrolled sepsis from infected limb
  • Paresis / irreversible ischaemia
  • Limited life expectancy (palliation)
  • Failed/impossible revascularisation

Conservative
  • 🚬 Smoking cessation — single biggest modifiable risk factor
  • 🏃 Exercise (supervised programme for claudication)
  • 🥗 Diet · weight loss
  • Optimise diabetes and hypertension
Medical
  • 💊 Atorvastatin 80 mg — all established CVD
  • 💊 Clopidogrel 75 mg — first-line antiplatelet; aspirin if intolerant
  • 💊 Naftidrofuryl — for claudication (if exercise fails)
  • ACEi / ARB for BP control

Maximising Manoeuvres

Right-sided → Inspiration (RILE)

  • Inspiration ↑ venous return → ↑ right heart flow → louder right-sided murmurs
  • TR, TS, pulmonary murmurs all louder in inspiration

Left-sided → Expiration

  • Expiration ↑ pulmonary venous return → ↑ left heart flow
  • AS, MR, MS, AR all louder in expiration
  • MS: also louder left lateral decubitus (brings apex closer to chest wall)
  • AR: sit forward, breath held in expiration
Other manoeuvres: Valsalva ↑ HOCM & MVP murmurs (↓ preload); squatting ↓ HOCM & MVP murmurs (↑ preload). AS radiates to carotids — always listen there. MR radiates to axilla.
Heart Sounds Primer
S1

Mitral & tricuspid closure (systole starts). Louder in MS (rigid but mobile valves snapping shut). Soft in MR (valve doesn't close properly).

S2

Aortic & pulmonary closure. Split on inspiration (pulmonary closes later). Soft/absent in severe AS. Wide fixed split in ASD. Loud in pulmonary HTN.

S3

Rapid ventricular filling. Physiological in young/athletic/pregnancy. Pathological in HF (LV dilatation) and severe MR. A "gallop" rhythm.

S4

Always pathological. Atrial contraction against stiff/non-compliant ventricle. Heard in AS (pressure overload), HCM, hypertension, ischaemic disease.

Opening snap (MS): follows S2; the earlier it occurs after S2, the higher the LA pressure and the more severe the stenosis.
Pericardial knock (constrictive pericarditis): sounds like S3 but earlier and louder — caused by abrupt halt to ventricular filling.
