Aortic Stenosis
The most common valvular lesion in developed countries. Ejection systolic murmur radiating to carotids. Symptoms = SAD.
Aetiology

Common Causes

  • Senile calcific — elderly (>65 yrs); calcium deposits on normal tricuspid valve; most common overall
  • Bicuspid aortic valve — presents in middle age (40–60 yrs); congenital; also causes AR
  • Rheumatic fever — post-streptococcal; tends to affect mitral first; causes commissural fusion

Mimics of AS Murmur (not true AS)

  • HOCM — dynamic obstruction; murmur ↑ with Valsalva, ↓ with squatting; does NOT radiate to carotids
  • Supravalvular AS — Coarctation-type lesion above valve; Williams syndrome
  • Subvalvular AS — fibromuscular shelf below valve; associated with AR
  • Aortic sclerosis — calcification without obstruction; normal S2, no symptoms
Pathophysiology
Narrowed valve → fixed outflow obstruction → LV must generate ↑ pressure to eject → concentric LV hypertrophy (compensatory; preserves wall stress) → ↑ oxygen demand → subendocardial ischaemia → eventually LV fails → ↓ stroke volume → ↓ cardiac output
Pressure overload → concentric hypertrophy → stiff, non-compliant LV → raised LVEDP → diastolic dysfunction → dyspnoea
Subendocardial ischaemia → angina even with normal coronaries → syncope on exertion (vasodilation + fixed CO)
Symptoms — SAD Triad
S
Syncope
Exertional. Fixed CO + vasodilation → cerebral underperfusion. Worst prognosis: survival ~2–3 years.
A
Angina
Exertional. Subendocardial ischaemia from ↑ demand + ↓ supply. Survival ~5 years.
D
Dyspnoea
Exertional → orthopnoea/PND. LV failure, raised LVEDP. Worst median survival ~2 years.
Key principle: Once symptoms develop, prognosis is poor without surgery. Asymptomatic AS (even severe) has much better prognosis than symptomatic AS.
Signs
Murmur: Ejection systolic (crescendo-decrescendo), loudest at right 2nd ICS, radiates to carotids. A4 is preceded by an ejection click (if valvular, not calcified).

AS Triad on Pulse/Sounds:
• Slow-rising (parvus et tardus) pulse — small amplitude, slow upstroke
• Narrow pulse pressure — ↓ stroke volume
• Soft / absent S2 — calcified immobile valve cannot produce a crisp closure sound

S4 — atrial kick against stiff, hypertrophied LV
Heaving (sustained, non-displaced) apex beat — concentric hypertrophy
Systolic thrill at base (severe AS)
Danger: As AS becomes very severe, the murmur may become quieter (failing LV → ↓ stroke volume → less turbulence). Do not be reassured by a soft murmur in a sick patient.
Investigations

Echo (key investigation)

  • Doppler gradient across valve — severe AS: mean gradient >40 mmHg / peak >64 mmHg, AVA <1 cm²
  • LV hypertrophy, function, wall motion
  • Bicuspid valve morphology
  • Serial echo every 1–2 years if asymptomatic severe

Other

  • ECG: LVH (tall R in V5–6, deep S in V1–2; strain pattern — ST depression + T inversion in lateral leads)
  • CXR: calcified aortic valve (lateral film); post-stenotic dilatation of ascending aorta; LVH → boot-shaped heart
  • Cardiac catheterisation: if echo inconclusive; pre-op coronary angiography
  • BNP: rising BNP in asymptomatic AS predicts symptom onset

ECG: left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) — tall R waves V5–6, deep S V1–2, lateral ST depression and T-wave inversion (strain pattern); classic finding in pressure-overloaded LV from AS

Management

Surgical AVR (SAVR)

  • Gold standard for most patients
  • Indicated if: symptomatic severe AS (SAD criteria) OR severe AS with mean gradient >40 mmHg OR EF <50%
  • Mechanical (younger) or bioprosthetic (older) valve

TAVI (Transcatheter AVR)

  • Transfemoral catheter-based valve implantation
  • For high surgical risk patients (frail, elderly, co-morbidities)
  • Now increasingly used in intermediate and even lower-risk patients
  • No open-chest surgery required

Balloon Aortic Valvuloplasty

  • Temporary measure only — high restenosis rate
  • Role: bridge to definitive AVR/TAVI in haemodynamically unstable patients
  • Not a definitive treatment
Medical management: No drug proven to slow AS progression. Diuretics for symptoms only. Vasodilators and nitrates are relatively contraindicated (fixed obstruction → severe hypotension if afterload dropped).
Mitral Regurgitation
Pansystolic murmur at apex radiating to axilla. Chronic (well-tolerated) vs acute (emergency).
Aetiology

Causes by Region / Age

  • Mitral valve prolapse (MVP) — most common in developed world; myxomatous degeneration; click + late systolic murmur (Barlow's)
  • Rheumatic fever — most common cause worldwide; fibrosis + commissural fusion
  • Infective endocarditis — valve leaflet destruction; can cause acute MR
  • Ischaemic — papillary muscle rupture (acute, post-STEMI) or ischaemia (chronic functional MR)
  • Connective tissue disorders — Marfan's, Ehlers-Danlos (myxomatous)
  • Functional MR — LV dilatation (any cause of DCM) → annulus dilatation; leaflets normal

Acute vs Chronic MR

  • Acute: IE, papillary muscle rupture, chordae tendineae rupture, chest trauma. LV and LA have no time to dilate → sudden ↑ LA pressure → acute pulmonary oedema. Emergency surgery.
  • Chronic: gradual LV and LA dilatation (compensatory) → large regurgitant volume tolerated for years → eventually LV fails (volume overload). Exertional dyspnoea, AF, emboli.
Pathophysiology
Incompetent mitral valve → systolic regurgitation into LA → ↑ LA volume and pressure → LA dilatation → AF → pulmonary hypertension → right heart failure. Meanwhile LV handles ↑ preload → eccentric LV dilatation (volume overload) → ↑ stroke volume compensates → eventually LV fails.
Regurgitant fraction: the proportion of stroke volume going backwards into LA. In severe MR this can be >50% — LV ejects twice what it needs to to maintain forward output.
AF: LA dilatation stretches the atrial myocardium → triggers AF. Once AF develops, LA thrombus + embolic risk → anticoagulate.
Symptoms

Chronic MR

  • Exertional dyspnoea (progressive)
  • Fatigue (↓ forward CO)
  • Palpitations (AF)
  • Peripheral oedema (RHF)
  • Embolic events (AF + LA thrombus)
  • Often asymptomatic for many years

Acute MR (Emergency)

  • Sudden severe pulmonary oedema
  • Cardiogenic shock
  • Cause usually evident: IE, post-MI (papillary muscle rupture), trauma
  • Murmur may be soft or inaudible (equalization of pressures)
  • Requires urgent surgical repair/replacement
Signs
Murmur: Pansystolic (throughout systole, from S1 to S2), blowing, high-pitched at the apex, radiating to axilla. Louder in expiration and with patient in left lateral decubitus.

• Soft S1 — valve doesn't close completely; closure sound attenuated
• S3 — rapid ventricular filling from enlarged LA; sign of significant MR
• Displaced, diffuse apex beat — LV volume overload → eccentric dilatation; apex down and out
• Signs of AF: irregularly irregular pulse
• Signs of pulmonary HTN / right HF in severe chronic MR
Investigations

Echo (key)

  • Quantifies severity (regurgitant fraction, vena contracta, ERO area)
  • LV dimensions and function — triggers for surgery
  • TOE if TTE inadequate or pre-operative
  • Serial echo: 6–12 monthly in moderate-severe

Other

  • ECG: AF; P mitrale (bifid P if sinus); LVH
  • CXR: LA enlargement (double heart border, widened carina); pulmonary oedema; cardiomegaly
  • Cardiac MRI: quantifies regurgitant volume if echo inadequate
  • BNP: useful marker of LV stress
Management

Medical

  • Treat heart failure: ACEi / ARB (reduce afterload, ↓ regurgitant fraction), diuretics, beta-blockers
  • Rate control / anticoagulation if AF (CHADS₂-VASc)
  • Serial echo surveillance
  • IE prophylaxis not routinely recommended (UK)

Surgical — Indications

  • Symptomatic severe MR with preserved EF
  • Asymptomatic severe MR with: LV dilatation (LVESD >45 mm), EF <60%, AF or pulmonary HTN
  • Repair preferred over replacement when anatomically feasible (lower mortality, no anticoagulation)
  • Acute severe MR → emergency surgery
MitraClip: percutaneous leaflet repair; option for very high surgical risk patients with severe symptomatic MR.
Mitral Stenosis
Rheumatic. Rheumatic. Rheumatic. Mid-diastolic rumble + opening snap. Louder leaning left, on expiration.
Aetiology

Rheumatic Fever (overwhelming majority)

  • Almost all MS is rheumatic in origin — often 10–20 years after the initial illness
  • Post-streptococcal Group A (GAS) pharyngitis → immune-mediated cardiac inflammation → valve fibrosis + commissural fusion + chordal shortening
  • Mitral valve affected in >90% of rheumatic heart disease; often with MR also
  • Rare non-rheumatic causes: congenital MS, large LA myxoma (mimics), systemic lupus (Libman-Sacks)
MS is becoming increasingly rare in developed countries as rheumatic fever rates have fallen. Still prevalent in developing world.
Pathophysiology
Fibrotic, fused mitral valve → fixed obstruction to LA emptying → ↑ LA pressure → LA dilatation → AF → LA thrombus/emboli. Simultaneously: raised LA pressure → pulmonary venous hypertension → pulmonary arterial hypertension → right heart failure. LV is actually underfilled and often normal or small.
LA dilatation
→ AF → thrombus → systemic embolism (stroke)
Pulmonary HTN
→ RV pressure overload → RV hypertrophy → RHF
↓ LV filling
→ ↓ cardiac output → fatigue, exertional dyspnoea
Symptoms

Symptoms from ↑ LA Pressure

  • Exertional dyspnoea (progressive) → orthopnoea, PND
  • Haemoptysis (pulmonary venous congestion)
  • Pulmonary oedema (especially tachycardia, pregnancy, infection)
  • Right heart failure symptoms: oedema, ascites

Symptoms from AF / Emboli

  • Palpitations (AF — irregular, often precipitates acute decompensation)
  • Stroke / TIA / peripheral emboli (LA thrombus)
  • Fatigue (↓ CO)
  • May remain asymptomatic for years if mild-moderate
Signs
Murmur: Mid-diastolic, low-pitched rumble, best heard at the apex with patient in left lateral decubitus, using the bell, on expiration. Presystolic accentuation if in sinus rhythm (atrial kick). Opening snap heard just after S2 (earlier snap = higher LA pressure = more severe).

• Loud S1 — forceful closure of stiff (but still mobile) mitral leaflets
• Low-volume pulse — fixed obstruction → ↓ stroke volume
• Malar flush (mitral facies) — butterfly erythema of cheeks; chronic low CO + pulmonary HTN → peripheral vasodilation + venous congestion
• Irregularly irregular pulse (AF is very common)
• Signs of right HF in advanced disease (↑JVP, oedema, hepatomegaly)
• Tapping apex beat — palpable loud S1; non-displaced (LV is normal)
Investigations

Echo (key)

  • Leaflet thickening/calcification, subvalvular disease, commissural fusion
  • Mitral valve area (MVA): severe if <1 cm²
  • Mean gradient across valve (severe: >10 mmHg)
  • LA size (dilatation), LA thrombus (TOE more sensitive)
  • Pulmonary artery pressure estimate

Other

  • ECG: P mitrale — bifid (notched) P wave in II (>120 ms), broad P in V1; AF; right axis deviation (RVH from pulmonary HTN)
  • CXR: LA enlargement (left atrial appendage, double right heart border, widened carina); pulmonary venous congestion (Kerley B lines); pulmonary oedema; mitral valve calcification
  • Cardiac catheterisation: if echo insufficient; pulmonary capillary wedge pressure
Management

Medical

  • Rate control (beta-blocker, digoxin, rate-limiting CCB) — slowing HR allows more time for diastolic filling across the stenotic valve
  • Anticoagulation (warfarin) — all patients with MS + AF; high embolic risk even with CHADS₂-VASc = 0 in MS
  • Diuretics for congestion/dyspnoea
  • Penicillin prophylaxis if history of rheumatic fever

Interventional

  • Percutaneous balloon mitral valvotomy (valvuloplasty) — first-line if anatomy suitable (pliable non-calcified leaflets, no significant MR, no LA thrombus); immediate haemodynamic improvement
  • Surgical mitral commissurotomy / valve replacement — if anatomy unsuitable for balloon, or severe MR coexists
  • Indications: symptomatic moderate-severe MS (MVA <1.5 cm²) OR pulmonary HTN OR new AF
Aortic Regurgitation
Wide pulse pressure → all eponymous signs. Early diastolic murmur at left sternal edge, leaning forward, expiration.
Aetiology

Valve / Leaflet Disease

  • Rheumatic fever — fibrosis + retraction of leaflets (often with MS)
  • Bicuspid aortic valve — congenital; causes both AS and AR
  • Infective endocarditis — leaflet perforation / destruction; acute AR
  • Collagen vascular disease (SLE, RA)

Aortic Root Disease (Dilatation)

  • Aortic dissection — acute emergency; dissection extends to aortic root
  • Marfan syndrome — cystic medial necrosis → aortic root dilatation
  • Syphilitic aortitis — obliterative endarteritis of vasa vasorum; classic cause
  • Hypertension — chronic aortic root dilatation
  • Ankylosing spondylitis, Reiter's syndrome, relapsing polychondritis
Acute AR emergencies: IE (leaflet destruction) and aortic dissection (root involvement) — both cause acute haemodynamic collapse. Emergency surgery.
Pathophysiology
Incompetent aortic valve → diastolic regurgitation into LV → ↑ LV end-diastolic volume → eccentric LV dilatation (volume overload, same as MR) → compensatory ↑ stroke volume → maintains forward output for years → LV eventually dilates and fails.
Wide pulse pressure: regurgitation ↓ diastolic BP (blood runs back into LV); compensatory ↑ SV → ↑ systolic BP. All peripheral signs flow from this single haemodynamic fact.
Acute AR: LV has no time to dilate; acute ↑ LVEDP → ↑↑ LA pressure → acute pulmonary oedema. Murmur may be short/soft as pressures equalize rapidly.
Symptoms

Chronic AR

  • Asymptomatic for years (compensated LV dilatation)
  • Exertional dyspnoea (progressive as LV fails)
  • Awareness of heartbeat (wide pulse pressure, hyperdynamic circulation)
  • Angina (↑ O₂ demand + ↓ diastolic coronary filling pressure)
  • Orthopnoea / PND (LV failure)

Acute AR

  • Sudden-onset acute pulmonary oedema
  • Cardiogenic shock
  • Cause: IE or aortic dissection
  • Emergency surgery required
Signs — The Eponym Parade
Murmur: Early diastolic, blowing, high-pitched, decrescendo — best heard at the left sternal edge, with patient sitting forward, breath held in expiration, using the diaphragm. Also a systolic ejection murmur (increased flow across aortic valve from large SV).

Austin Flint murmur: Mid-diastolic rumble at apex — regurgitant jet impinges on anterior mitral leaflet, causing functional MS; can be confused with true MS (no opening snap in Austin Flint).

Peripheral Signs — all explained by wide pulse pressure:

Corrigan's / Water-Hammer Pulse

Rapid upstroke and collapse; felt at the wrist and carotids. Lift the arm — exaggerated pulsation. = Collapsing pulse.

Quincke's Sign

Capillary pulsation visible at the nail-bed (press lightly on nail). Systolic flushing + diastolic blanching from wide PP.

de Musset's Sign

Head nodding with each heartbeat. Carotid hyperdynamic pulsation moves the head. (Musset was a French poet with AR.)

Duroziez's Sign

Femoral artery: systolic and diastolic murmur heard on partial compression with stethoscope. Retrograde diastolic flow.

Traube's Sign

"Pistol-shot" sound heard over femoral artery. Hyperdynamic systolic pulsation.

Hill's Sign

BP in legs exceeds arm by >20 mmHg. Popliteal systolic BP > brachial. Significant in severe AR.

Displaced, diffuse apex beat — down and out (volume overload → eccentric LV dilatation). The apex beat of AR is described as "heaving and displaced."
Investigations

Echo

  • Quantifies severity (PHT, vena contracta, ERO)
  • LV dimensions: surgery if LVEDD >70 mm or LVESD >50 mm
  • LV systolic function (EF) — key surgical trigger
  • Aortic root diameter and morphology
  • Serial 6–12 monthly if moderate-severe

Other

  • ECG: LVH (volume overload pattern — tall voltage); AF possible
  • CXR: cardiomegaly (LV dilatation); ± aortic root dilatation/unfolded aorta
  • CT aorta: if dissection suspected or root dilatation (>45 mm)
  • Cardiac MRI: most accurate for quantifying regurgitant volume
Management

Medical

  • Vasodilators / ACEi — ↓ afterload → ↓ regurgitant fraction; indicated if LV dilatation / hypertension / not surgical candidate
  • Diuretics for symptoms
  • Monitor BP — aortic root dilatation → target <130/80
  • Beta-blockers: avoid (↑ diastolic time → ↑ regurgitation duration)

Surgical AVR — Indications

  • Symptomatic severe AR
  • Asymptomatic severe AR with: EF <50%, LVESD >50 mm, LVEDD >70 mm
  • Operate before irreversible LV dysfunction — once EF falls permanently surgery is still beneficial but risk increases
  • Acute severe AR (IE, dissection) → emergency surgery
Right-sided Valvular Disease & Exam Pearls
Lower-yield but still tested. Plus the cross-cutting pearls to pull everything together.
Tricuspid Regurgitation (TR)

Aetiology

  • Functional (most common) — RV dilatation from any cause (pulmonary HTN, RV failure) → annular dilatation → leaflets normal
  • Rheumatic fever (usually with MS/MR)
  • IE — especially IVDU (right-sided IE)
  • Carcinoid syndrome (plaques on tricuspid/pulmonary valves)
  • Congenital (Ebstein's anomaly — tricuspid displaced into RV)

Features

  • Pansystolic murmur at lower left sternal edge, louder on inspiration
  • Giant V waves in JVP — systolic regurgitation into RA → large V wave
  • Pulsatile / enlarged liver — systolic regurgitation transmitted to hepatic veins
  • Peripheral oedema, ascites (RHF)
  • ↑ JVP
  • Management: treat underlying cause; diuretics; surgery if severe and refractory
Tricuspid Stenosis (TS)

Rare. Almost always rheumatic (almost always with MS). Fixed obstruction → ↑ RA pressure → RA dilatation → giant a waves in JVP (prominent atrial contraction against obstruction). Diastolic murmur at left sternal edge, louder on inspiration. Hepatomegaly, ascites, oedema without pulmonary congestion (blocked upstream of lungs). Treat with balloon valvuloplasty or surgical commissurotomy.

Pulmonary Regurgitation & Stenosis

Pulmonary Regurgitation

  • Graham Steell murmur — early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge; due to pulmonary regurgitation secondary to pulmonary hypertension (most common cause)
  • Congenital; post-surgical (ToF repair)
  • Usually benign but can cause RV dilatation and failure over time
  • Louder on inspiration

Pulmonary Stenosis

  • Usually congenital (isolated or part of Fallot's tetralogy, Noonan's)
  • Ejection systolic murmur at left upper sternal edge + ejection click
  • Louder on inspiration
  • Signs of RV pressure overload: heave, raised JVP
  • Mild-moderate: excellent prognosis. Severe: balloon valvuloplasty
⭐ Exam Pearls
Murmur radiation: AS → carotids; MR → axilla. Always examine neck and axilla when you hear a murmur.
RILE: Right-sided louder Inspiration, Left-sided louder Expiration. For maximising any murmur on examination.
AS symptoms = SAD (Syncope, Angina, Dyspnoea — all exertional). Once SAD develops, prognosis poor without surgery.
AS triad: slow-rising pulse + narrow pulse pressure + soft S2. S4 from stiff hypertrophied LV.
Wide pulse pressure → AR. All eponyms (Corrigan's, Quincke's, de Musset's, Duroziez's, Hill's) explained by wide PP alone.
P mitrale = MS (bifid P in lead II, >120 ms). Austin Flint murmur = AR mimicking MS (no opening snap).
Bicuspid aortic valve → AS in middle age (calcification) AND AR (leaflet dysfunction). Screen for aortic root dilatation.
Acute severe MR or AR = emergency (pulmonary oedema). Causes: IE (leaflet destruction), aortic dissection (AR), papillary muscle rupture (MR).
Rheumatic fever thread: MS → MR → AR → TS/TR. Almost all MS is rheumatic; treat with penicillin prophylaxis.
Opening snap in MS: earlier snap = higher LA pressure = more severe stenosis. No opening snap = heavily calcified immobile leaflets.
Graham Steell murmur = pulmonary regurgitation from pulmonary HTN (secondary to MS). Early diastolic at left sternal edge.
Operate on AR before irreversible LV dysfunction: if EF <50% or LVESD >50 mm even if asymptomatic — don't wait for symptoms.

Tachycardia — Overview & Classification

Tachycardia is defined as a heart rate >100 bpm. The first and most important ECG step is to measure the QRS duration:

Narrow QRS (<120 ms)
Supraventricular origin — impulse uses normal His-Purkinje system
Regular
  • Sinus tachycardia
  • AVNRT — re-entry within AV node
  • AVRT — re-entry via accessory pathway
  • Atrial tachycardia
  • Atrial flutter (fixed block) — e.g. 2:1
Irregular
  • Atrial fibrillation
  • Atrial flutter (variable block)
  • Multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT)
Broad QRS (≥120 ms)
Broad-complex width — ventricular until proven otherwise; the QRS width, not origin, triggers this rule
Regular
  • Ventricular tachycardia (VT) — most likely
  • SVT with aberrant conduction (BBB)
  • SVT with pre-excitation (WPW)
Irregular
  • Pre-excited AF (WPW + AF) — danger!
  • Torsades de pointes / polymorphic VT
  • AF with BBB
⚡ Key rule
Broad complex tachycardia = VT until proven otherwise. Never assume SVT + aberrancy without senior review.
✔ Narrow = safe
A narrow QRS guarantees supraventricular origin — the ventricles are activated normally via His-Purkinje.
⚠ WPW + AF
Pre-excited AF can cause a broad, irregular tachycardia that mimics VF — do NOT give AV nodal blockers.
ECG Diagnostic Framework — How to Read a Tachycardia

A systematic approach to any tachycardia (HR >100 bpm). Follow the steps in order — Step 2 is a hard fork: broad-complex rhythms go directly to the VT feature checklist, not to P-wave analysis.

1️⃣
Regular or Irregular?
Count R-R intervals across a 6-second strip.
• Completely irregular (no pattern) → AF or multifocal atrial tachycardia (MAT)
• Irregular with a pattern (e.g. varying groups) → atrial flutter with variable block
• Regular → proceed to Step 2
↓
2️⃣
Narrow (<120 ms) or Broad (≥120 ms) QRS?
This is the critical fork — it determines the entire management pathway.
Narrow QRS → Step 3: P-wave analysis
Normal P before each QRS → sinus tachycardia (treat the cause)
Absent P + chaotic baseline → AF (fibrillatory f-waves)
Sawtooth at ~300 bpm (best in II, III, aVF, V1) → atrial flutter
Buried P (pseudo-R' in V1, pseudo-S in II/aVF) → AVNRT
P after QRS (RP < PR) → AVRT (accessory pathway)
Abnormal P morphology, rate 100–250 → atrial tachycardia
⚠ Broad QRS → VT until proven otherwise — look for VT features
Do NOT proceed to P-wave analysis. Instead check for:

AV dissociation — P waves march through independently → diagnostic of VT
Capture beats — rare narrow QRS amid broad → diagnostic of VT
Fusion beats — hybrid morphology → diagnostic of VT
Concordance — all V leads deflect same direction
Atypical BBB morphology — doesn't match classic LBBB/RBBB pattern
Structural heart disease / prior MI — strongly favours VT

If uncertain: treat as VT. Never give verapamil to broad-complex tachycardia.
Stability Override — Treat the Patient, Not the Rhythm

Regardless of rhythm diagnosis, haemodynamic instability = immediate synchronised DC cardioversion (or defibrillation for pulseless VT/VF). Do not delay to identify the rhythm.

⚡ What does unstable look like?
  • Hypotension — SBP <90 mmHg
  • Reduced consciousness — confusion, syncope, GCS drop
  • Ischaemic chest pain — not palpitations alone
  • Acute pulmonary oedema — severe breathlessness, crepitations
Note: Palpitations, anxiety, and mild breathlessness alone do not constitute instability. The threshold is end-organ compromise or haemodynamic collapse.
Stable → time to identify rhythm, consider pharmacological options, vagal manoeuvres
Unstable → call for help · IV access · synchronised DC shock · sedation if conscious
"Is the AV Node in the Circuit?" — The Treatment Principle

The most important conceptual question for any stable tachycardia. It determines whether AV nodal blocking agents (adenosine, beta-blockers, verapamil, diltiazem) will terminate, slow, or endanger the patient.

✔ Node IS in re-entry circuit
Nodal blockers → terminate the rhythm
  • AVNRT
  • AVRT (orthodromic)
~ Rate control only
Node conducts but doesn't sustain circuit — blockers slow rate, do not terminate
  • AF — atria sustain it; node is gatekeeper
  • Atrial flutter — macro re-entry in atria only
  • Atrial tachycardia — ectopic atrial focus
  • Sinus tachycardia — treat the cause
⚠ Node NOT in circuit
Nodal blockers → dangerous or useless
  • VT — may cause arrest
  • Pre-excited AF (WPW) — blocking AV node forces all conduction down accessory pathway → VF
  • Antidromic AVRT — use procainamide / flecainide
🔑 Key mnemonic: Narrow + regular + no pre-excitation → AV-node-dependent → adenosine safe and likely terminates. Any broad-complex tachycardia → treat as VT; never give verapamil to a broad-complex rhythm.

Irregular Narrow-Complex Tachycardias — Defining Features
All three share: narrow QRS (<120 ms) · irregularly irregular rhythm · no consistent P–QRS relationship · AV node is a bystander, not part of the circuit
AF
  • No P waves
  • Chaotic fibrillatory baseline (f-waves, best in V1)
  • Completely irregular R-R intervals
Variable-Block Flutter
  • Sawtooth flutter waves ~300 bpm (best in II, III, aVF)

MAT

2A — Atrial Fibrillation
Definition & Mechanism

AF is disorganised atrial electrical activity driven by multiple chaotic micro re-entry wavelets — there is no single focus and no coordinated contraction. The key consequences:

Haemodynamic
Loss of atrial kick → cardiac output ↓ 10–20% (worse in diastolic dysfunction)
Thromboembolic
Stasis in left atrial appendage → thrombus → stroke/TIA (risk ×5 vs general population)
Tachycardia-mediated
Sustained fast ventricular rate → cardiomyopathy if untreated for months
Classification
Paroxysmal — self-terminating <7 days (usually <48h). Sinus rhythm restored spontaneously.
Persistent — duration >7 days; requires cardioversion to restore sinus rhythm.
Long-standing persistent — >12 months; rhythm control still being attempted.
Permanent — cardioversion abandoned; rate control and anticoagulation only.
Valvular vs Non-valvular: Valvular AF = AF with moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis or mechanical heart valve. This distinction matters — valvular AF requires warfarin (VKA); DOACs are contraindicated. All other AF is non-valvular → DOACs preferred.
Causes — SMITH
S
Sepsis · Surgery (post-operative AF, esp. cardiac) · Sleep apnoea
M
Mitral valve disease (MS, MR) — chronic pressure/volume overload dilates LA
I
IHD / MI · Inflammation (pericarditis, myocarditis) · Idiopathic (lone AF, young patients)
T
Thyroid — hyperthyroidism (always check TFTs in new AF)
H
Hypertension — most common modifiable cause worldwide
Also: Alcohol (holiday heart syndrome — binge drinking triggers paroxysmal AF) · PE · COPD / pneumonia · Obesity · HF / cardiomyopathy · Caffeine and stimulants (minor risk)
ECG Features
  • Irregularly irregular rhythm — no two R-R intervals are equal (hallmark)
  • Absent P waves — replaced by fibrillatory f-waves (fine irregular oscillations, best seen in V1 and lead II); atrial rate 350–600 bpm
  • Narrow QRS — unless concurrent BBB or pre-excitation (WPW)
  • Ventricular rate — typically 100–160 bpm untreated; AV node filters the chaotic atrial impulses
  • No isoelectric baseline between QRS complexes
Acute Management
Unstable (haemodynamically compromised): immediate synchronised DC cardioversion regardless of onset time. Do not delay for anticoagulation.
Rate Control (stable)
  • Beta-blockers — bisoprolol, metoprolol (first-line; avoid in decompensated HF)
  • CCB — diltiazem or verapamil (if BB contraindicated; avoid in HFrEF)
  • Digoxin — sedentary patients, HF with AF; poor rate control on exertion
  • Target: HR <110 bpm at rest (lenient); <80 bpm if symptomatic
Rhythm Control (cardioversion)
  • <48h onset (or anticoagulated ≥3 weeks) → cardiovert safely
  • >48h or unknown onset → TOE to exclude LA appendage thrombus, OR anticoagulate ≥3 weeks before, then ≥4 weeks after cardioversion
  • Chemical: flecainide (no structural heart disease) · amiodarone (structural disease / HF)
  • Electrical: synchronised DC shock (start 120–150 J biphasic)

2B — Atrial Flutter with Variable Block
Mechanism

Macro re-entry circuit circulating around the tricuspid annulus. The cavotricuspid isthmus (CTI) — the tissue between the tricuspid valve and inferior vena cava — is the critical slow zone. Ablating this isthmus breaks the circuit.

  • Atrial rate: ~300 bpm (range 250–350)
  • Sawtooth flutter waves — inverted in II, III, aVF; upright in V1
  • No isoelectric baseline between flutter waves
  • Variable AV block → irregular ventricular response (this section)
  • Fixed 2:1 block → ventricular rate ~150, regular (→ §3 Regular Narrow)
Management
  • Rate control — same agents as AF (beta-blockers, CCBs, digoxin); flutter can be harder to rate-control pharmacologically
  • Anticoagulation — same CHA₂DS₂-VASc thresholds as AF; stroke risk equivalent
  • Cardioversion — flutter is often more responsive than AF; lower energy needed (50–100 J biphasic). Same <48h / >48h anticoagulation rule applies.
  • CTI ablation — curative in ~95% of typical flutter; first-line for recurrent or persistent flutter
→ Fixed 2:1 flutter (regular, rate ~150) — see §3 Regular Narrow-Complex Tachycardias
2C — Multifocal Atrial Tachycardia (MAT)
Definition & ECG
  • ≥3 distinct P-wave morphologies in the same ECG lead
  • Varying PR intervals
  • Irregular rhythm, rate >100 bpm
  • Narrow QRS (unless aberrant conduction)
  • Mechanism: multiple ectopic atrial foci firing chaotically — NOT re-entry (cardioversion is ineffective)
Classic causes: COPD (most common) · Hypoxia · Hypomagnesaemia · Theophylline toxicity · Sepsis · Pulmonary hypertension
Management
  • Treat the underlying cause — oxygen for hypoxia, optimise COPD, correct Mg²⁺ and K⁺
  • Rate control — CCB preferred (verapamil or diltiazem); avoid beta-blockers in bronchospasm
  • Do NOT cardiovert — ineffective; multiple foci, not a single re-entry circuit
  • No routine anticoagulation — MAT does not carry the same stroke risk as AF/flutter; not a sustained atrial arrhythmia equivalent
⚠ Exam trap: MAT can be mistaken for AF — look carefully for distinct (if abnormal) P waves. AF has no identifiable P waves at all.
Shared Management Principles
AV Node = Bystander In all three rhythms the AV node is not part of the sustaining circuit. Block it to control ventricular rate, not to terminate the arrhythmia.
Anticoagulation AF and atrial flutter share equivalent stroke risk → use same CHA₂DS₂-VASc thresholds. MAT: no routine anticoagulation.
Rate Control Target HR <110 bpm at rest (lenient) for most patients. Stricter <80 bpm only if symptomatic at lenient rate. Treat the cause in MAT.
Regular Narrow-Complex Tachycardias — Defining Features
All five share: narrow QRS (<120 ms) · regular R–R intervals · rate >100 bpm
Group A — Re-entry (AV node IN circuit)
AVNRT · AVRT (orthodromic)
Vagal / adenosine → terminates
Group B — AV node bystander
Atrial tachycardia · Atrial flutter (fixed 2:1)
Adenosine diagnoses; rate control manages
Group C — Normal pacemaker
Sinus tachycardia
Treat the cause — never rate-block blindly
⚠ The 150 bpm trap: A regular narrow tachycardia at exactly 150 bpm → assume atrial flutter with fixed 2:1 block until proven otherwise. P waves may be hidden in T waves. Give adenosine to unmask the flutter waves.
Group A — Re-entry with AV Node IN the Circuit ("The True SVTs")
Shared principle: The AV node is an essential part of the re-entry circuit. Blocking it — with vagal manoeuvres or adenosine — terminates the arrhythmia. These are "AV-node-dependent" tachycardias.
3A.1 — AVNRT (Atrioventricular Nodal Re-entrant Tachycardia)

The most common paroxysmal SVT. Affects young adults, more common in women. Abrupt onset and offset ("on-off switch").

Mechanism
  • Two pathways within the AV node: slow (longer ERP) and fast (shorter ERP)
  • A premature atrial beat finds the fast pathway refractory → travels down the slow pathway → re-enters up the fast → sustained loop
  • Atria and ventricles activated nearly simultaneously (P buried in or just after QRS)
ECG Signature
  • Rate 140–280 bpm, regular
  • Narrow QRS (normal His-Purkinje activation)
  • P waves buried in QRS or immediately after → pseudo-R' in V1 (most useful sign) or pseudo-S in II/III/aVF
  • Short RP interval (RP < PR)
  • Abrupt onset; often triggered by a PAC
AVNRT: narrow QRS complexes, P waves not visible (buried in QRS)
Treatment
Step 1 — Vagal manoeuvres
Valsalva (modified — legs elevated) or carotid sinus massage. Terminates ~25% of episodes.
Step 2 — Adenosine IV
6 mg rapid IV bolus; if no response: 12 mg, then 18 mg. Transiently blocks AV node → terminates circuit. Warn patient: flushing, chest tightness, brief asystole (seconds). Contraindicated in asthma / high-degree AV block.
Step 3 — If adenosine fails
Verapamil 2.5–5 mg IV (not if broad complex or pre-excitation) · Metoprolol IV · Synchronised DC cardioversion if haemodynamically unstable.
Long-term / recurrent AVNRT: Flecainide or beta-blocker for prevention; slow-pathway catheter ablation is curative (>95% success, low risk of AV block).
3A.2 — AVRT, Orthodromic (Atrioventricular Re-entrant Tachycardia)

Re-entry using an accessory pathway (e.g. Bundle of Kent in WPW). Orthodromic = conduction down the AV node and up the accessory pathway → narrow QRS (normal ventricular activation).

Mechanism
  • Impulse travels: SA node → AV node → His-Purkinje → ventricles (narrow QRS) → retrograde up accessory pathway → atria → AV node again
  • P wave occurs after QRS (retrograde atrial activation)
  • Associated with WPW syndrome (delta wave + short PR in sinus rhythm)
ECG Signature
  • Rate 150–250 bpm, regular, narrow QRS
  • P wave after QRS → RP < PR (inverted P in II/III/aVF)
  • Longer RP than AVNRT (P clearly visible after QRS, not buried)
  • In sinus rhythm: look for short PR + delta wave (WPW)
AVRT: Orthodromic vs Antidromic — Why QRS Width Differs
Orthodromic (~95%) — This section
  • Antegrade down the AV node → His-Purkinje → ventricles
  • Ventricles activated via normal wiring → narrow QRS
  • Retrograde up the accessory pathway → atria → loop repeats
  • Sits in §3 (Regular Narrow). Looks like ordinary SVT.
Antidromic (~5%) — §4C
  • Antegrade down the accessory pathway → straight into ventricular muscle
  • Bypasses His-Purkinje — abnormal, sequential spread → broad QRS
  • Retrograde up the AV node → atria → loop repeats
  • Sits in §4C (Regular Broad). Mimics VT.
“Ortho” = correct direction (down AV node) · “Anti” = opposite direction (down AP). The pathway taken determines QRS width.
Treatment: Same stepwise approach as AVNRT — vagal manoeuvres → adenosine → verapamil/beta-blocker → DC cardioversion if unstable. Definitive: accessory pathway ablation (curative). Long-term: avoid AV nodal blockers if WPW present in sinus rhythm (risk of pre-excited AF).
⚠ Antidromic AVRT (conduction down accessory pathway, up AV node) = broad complex — treated differently. See Regular Broad section.
Group B — AV Node a Bystander (Not the Circuit)
Shared principle: The AV node conducts the impulse to the ventricles but is not part of the sustaining circuit. Adenosine transiently blocks AV conduction → unmasks underlying atrial activity (diagnostic) but does not terminate. Manage with rate control.
3B.1 — Atrial Tachycardia
Mechanism & Features
  • Ectopic atrial focus firing faster than the sinus node (enhanced automaticity or micro re-entry)
  • Rate 100–250 bpm, regular
  • "Warm-up" onset — rate gradually accelerates at start (distinguishes from AVNRT/AVRT which are abrupt)
  • Abnormal P-wave morphology — differs from sinus P in same lead; P axis depends on focus location
  • PR interval normal or prolonged (AV node not part of circuit)
  • Causes: structural heart disease, digoxin toxicity, alcohol, hypoxia
Treatment
  • Treat underlying cause (especially digoxin toxicity — stop digoxin)
  • Rate control: beta-blockers or CCBs
  • Adenosine: may transiently block AV node and reveal atrial activity but rarely terminates
  • Rhythm control if needed: flecainide, amiodarone
  • Focal catheter ablation if recurrent and drug-refractory
3B.2 — Atrial Flutter, Fixed 2:1 Block
ECG Signature
  • Atrial rate ~300 bpm, fixed 2:1 AV block → ventricular rate ~150 bpm, regular
  • Sawtooth flutter waves — inverted in II, III, aVF; upright in V1
  • Flutter waves may be hidden in T waves at 2:1 — look carefully
  • The 150 bpm rule: any regular narrow tachycardia at 150 → consider flutter first
  • Adenosine increases AV block transiently → flutter waves become visible
Management
  • Rate control: beta-blockers, CCBs, digoxin (same as AF)
  • Anticoagulation: same CHA₂DS₂-VASc thresholds as AF
  • Cardioversion: highly effective, often lower energy than AF (50–100 J)
  • CTI ablation: curative ~95%
→ Variable-block flutter (irregular) — see §2 Irregular Narrow

Key principle: Sinus tachycardia is always a response to something — it is physiologically appropriate. Never rate-block it without identifying and treating the cause. Slowing the rate without addressing the driver can be dangerous.

  • Normal upright P wave before every QRS — identical morphology throughout
  • Normal PR interval (0.12–0.20 s)

⚡ The Golden Rule Treat every regular broad-complex tachycardia as VT until proven otherwise. Misdiagnosing VT as SVT and giving a nodal blocker (verapamil, diltiazem) can be fatal. Treating SVT as VT is always safe.

Broad QRS defined: ≥120 ms (3 small squares) · rate > 100 bpm · regular R–R intervals. Any of these three conditions can produce this pattern — history, ECG morphology, and haemodynamic context guide diagnosis.
4A — Ventricular Tachycardia (VT)
Mechanism
Pathophysiology
  • Impulse originates below the His bundle in ventricular myocardium
  • Spreads cell-to-cell (not via His-Purkinje) — slow, abnormal depolarisation → wide QRS
  • Most common substrate: re-entry around scar from prior MI / IHD
  • Also: structural heart disease, cardiomyopathy, channelopathies
  • Monomorphic VT (this section): same QRS morphology — stable re-entry circuit
  • Polymorphic VT / Torsades → see §5 (Irregular Broad)
Why IHD History is Critical
In any patient with known ischaemic heart disease or prior MI, a regular broad-complex tachycardia is VT until definitively proven otherwise. The scar provides the re-entry substrate. Prior MI raises the pre-test probability of VT to >95%.
Haemodynamic stability does NOT rule out VT. Patients can be in VT and remain haemodynamically stable — a common and dangerous trap.
ECG Features Favouring VT
High Specificity for VT
  • AV dissociation — P waves and QRS complexes march independently; pathognomonic when seen
  • Capture beats — occasional narrow QRS during VT as a sinus impulse briefly captures the ventricles
  • Fusion beats — hybrid QRS morphology when sinus and ventricular impulse collide simultaneously
  • Concordance — all precordial leads (V1–V6) point same direction (all positive or all negative)
Supportive Features
  • Very broad QRS (>140 ms) — the wider, the more likely VT
  • Extreme axis deviation — north-west axis (“no man’s land”, −90° to ±180°)
  • RS interval >100 ms in any precordial lead (Brugada criterion)
  • RBBB-like pattern but dominant S in V6 (not a tall R)
  • LBBB-like pattern but Q or R in V1 (not a pure negative deflection)
Management
⚠ Assess stability first. Unstable = any of: hypotension, shock, syncope, pulmonary oedema, ischaemic chest pain.
Unstable VT
  • Synchronised DC cardioversion immediately
  • Sedate first if conscious (midazolam / propofol)
  • If pulseless: treat as VF — unsynchronised defibrillation + CPR (arrest algorithm)
Stable VT
  • Amiodarone 300 mg IV over 20–60 min (first-line UK)
  • Then 900 mg over 24 h maintenance
  • Correct electrolytes: K⁺, Mg²⁺
  • Procainamide or lidocaine: alternatives where available
  • Prepare for cardioversion if drug therapy fails
4B — SVT with Aberrancy (Bundle Branch Block)
Mechanism
  • A supraventricular rhythm (AVNRT, AVRT, atrial tachycardia) conducts normally to the AV node
  • Below the AV node, conduction is blocked or delayed in one bundle branch
  • Ventricle depolarises via the opposite bundle — slow spread → broad QRS
  • Pre-existing BBB: present at baseline; same morphology in sinus rhythm
  • Rate-related (phase 3) BBB: appears only at faster rates when bundle’s refractory period is exceeded
How to Distinguish from VT
  • Classic RBBB or LBBB morphology (not atypical)
  • No AV dissociation, no capture or fusion beats
  • P waves visible and 1:1 with QRS
  • Identical morphology to prior 12-lead (if pre-existing BBB)
  • Narrow QRS at slower rate on previous ECG (if rate-related)
  • Terminates or slows with vagal manoeuvres / adenosine
Clinical bottom line: Adenosine is useful diagnostically here — but only if you are confident this is not VT (old 12-lead showing BBB, no structural heart disease, haemodynamically stable, classic SVT history). When in doubt, treat as VT.
Classic BBB morphology: RBBB (rSR’ in V1, qRs in V6) vs LBBB (rS in V1, R in V6). SVT with aberrancy shows one of these patterns — atypical morphology favours VT.
4C — Antidromic AVRT (WPW, SVT with Pre-excitation)
Mechanism
  • In WPW, the accessory pathway (AP) can conduct both antegrade and retrograde
  • Antidromic: impulse travels antegrade down the AP, then retrograde up the His-AV node
  • Ventricle depolarises entirely via the AP — maximally pre-excited → very broad, slurred QRS
  • Contrast with orthodromic AVRT (§3A.2): down AV node, up AP → narrow QRS
  • Uncommon — ∼5–10% of AVRT in WPW patients
ECG & Clinical Features
  • Broad, maximally pre-excited QRS (may resemble LBBB or be atypical)
  • Regular tachycardia, rate typically 150–250 bpm
  • No AV dissociation (AV node part of circuit retrogradely)
  • History of WPW or δ-wave on baseline ECG is diagnostic clue
  • If AF develops in WPW → see §5 (Irregular Broad) — life-threatening
⚠ Treatment danger: Nodal blockers (adenosine, verapamil, beta-blockers) block retrograde AV conduction — may force all conduction anterograde down the AP → risk of VF. Use flecainide or procainamide (or DC cardioversion).
VT vs SVT — Discriminator & Safety Rules
Favours VT
  • AV dissociation (pathognomonic)
  • Capture or fusion beats
  • Concordance in precordial leads
  • QRS >140 ms
  • Extreme / north-west axis
  • Known IHD or prior MI
  • Structural heart disease
  • Atypical BBB morphology
Favours SVT with Aberrancy
  • Classic RBBB or LBBB morphology
  • P waves clearly 1:1 with QRS
  • No AV dissociation / no capture / fusion
  • Identical to prior ECG with BBB
  • Young, no structural heart disease
  • Terminates with adenosine
  • Prior history of SVT, no syncope
① Stability first Unstable → synchronised DC cardioversion immediately, regardless of diagnosis
② Doubt = VT Cannot exclude VT confidently? Treat as VT — amiodarone IV. Never give verapamil or diltiazem blindly to a broad-complex tachycardia.
③ The unifying question “Could this be VT?” — If yes, treat it as VT. Step down only with clear evidence and specialist input.
Irregular Broad-Complex Tachycardias — Defining Features
⚠ The Danger Section Irregular and broad narrows to a short list of high-risk rhythms. The instinct to instil: irregular broad → think pre-excited AF or polymorphic VT until proven otherwise. Never reflexively give AV-nodal blockers — it can be fatal.

Broad QRS defined: ≥120 ms · rate > 100 bpm · irregular R–R intervals. Three conditions create this pattern — distinguishing them determines whether you give a nodal blocker or avoid it entirely.
5A — Pre-excited AF (WPW + AF) — The Lethal Trap
Mechanism
  • In WPW, the accessory pathway (AP) bypasses the AV node
  • Normally during SVT, the AV node rate-limits ventricular conduction (max ~180 bpm)
  • When AF develops in WPW, the chaotic atrial impulses conduct directly down the AP — bypassing the AV node’s protective gating
  • Ventricles are bombarded at near-atrial rates (300–600 bpm atrial, often >200 bpm ventricular)
  • Each beat may conduct via AP, AV node, or both → varying QRS width beat-to-beat (fusion beats)
  • Can degenerate to VF — immediately life-threatening
ECG Signature
  • Irregular R–R intervals (underlying AF)
  • Broad QRS (conducted via AP)
  • Very fast — ventricular rate often >200 bpm
  • Varying QRS width — beat-to-beat fusion as conduction varies between AP and AV node
  • No organised P waves (underlying AF)
  • Baseline WPW: short PR + δ wave in sinus rhythm (if seen prior)
Cross-ref: WPW in sinus rhythm → §3A.2 (orthodromic AVRT, narrow) · §4C (antidromic AVRT, broad)
Management
✘ NEVER give AV-nodal blockers: adenosine · verapamil · diltiazem · beta-blockers · digoxin. These block the AV node and force all conduction down the accessory pathway → extreme rate acceleration → VF.
Unstable
  • Synchronised DC cardioversion immediately
  • Sedate first if conscious
  • If degenerated to VF → unsynchronised defibrillation + CPR
Stable
  • Flecainide IV — first-line if no structural heart disease
  • Procainamide IV — alternative, safe with structural disease
  • Both work by slowing AP conduction, not blocking the AV node
  • Consider early cardioversion if drug response is slow
5B — Polymorphic VT / Torsades de Pointes
Mechanism
  • Polymorphic VT: VT with continuously varying QRS morphology and axis — irregular, “twisting around the baseline”
  • Torsades de Pointes = polymorphic VT occurring on a background of prolonged QT interval
  • Prolonged QT → prolonged repolarisation → spontaneous depolarisation in some cells (early after-depolarisations) → triggered VT
  • Typically self-terminating but can degenerate to VF
  • QT measured from start of QRS to end of T wave; corrected QT (QTc) >440 ms (men) / >460 ms (women) = prolonged
ECG Signature
  • Irregular broad-complex tachycardia
  • QRS complexes twist around the isoelectric baseline — amplitude waxes and wanes over 5–20 beats
  • Preceding sinus rhythm shows long QT (key diagnostic clue)
  • Rate typically 160–250 bpm
  • May self-terminate, recur, or degenerate to VF
Causes of Prolonged QT
Congenital
  • Long QT syndrome (LQTS) — channelopathy
  • Romano-Ward (autosomal dominant)
  • Jervell and Lange-Nielsen (+ deafness)
Drugs — High-Yield List
  • Antiarrhythmics: sotalol, amiodarone, quinidine/procainamide (Class Ia)
  • Antipsychotics: haloperidol, quetiapine
  • Antidepressants: citalopram, TCAs
  • Antibiotics: macrolides (erythromycin, clarithromycin)
  • Antiemetics: ondansetron, domperidone
  • Antimalarials: chloroquine, quinine
Electrolytes
  • Hypokalaemia — most common electrolyte cause
  • Hypomagnesaemia
  • Hypocalcaemia
  • All impair repolarisation → lengthen QT
Management
Unstable / Pulseless
  • Unsynchronised defibrillation (polymorphic → sync unreliable)
  • If pulseless → arrest algorithm
Stable Torsades
  • IV magnesium sulphate 2 g over 10 min — first-line, even if serum Mg²⁺ is normal
  • Correct electrolytes: K⁺ → >4.5 mmol/L, Mg²⁺ → >1 mmol/L, Ca²⁺
  • Stop all QT-prolonging drugs immediately
  • Treat underlying cause (electrolyte, drug, ischaemia)
  • Consider temporary pacing (overdrive pacing shortens QT)
  • ICD if recurrent / congenital LQTS
  • Avoid amiodarone — itself prolongs QT
⭐ Exam pearl: Magnesium works even when serum Mg²⁺ is normal — it stabilises cardiac membranes. Do NOT wait for a low level before giving it. Sotalol prolongs QT and causes torsades — do not confuse with other beta-blockers (which are safe and used in congenital LQTS).
5C — AF with Bundle Branch Block
Mechanism
  • Ordinary AF (irregular atrial activity) + pre-existing or rate-related BBB
  • The AF provides the irregularity; the BBB provides the broad QRS
  • The AV node is intact — rate-limiting still applies (ventricular rate rarely >180 bpm)
  • This is the “less scary” broad-irregular — it’s just AF that looks broad

Management: Once pre-excited AF is confidently excluded, manage as AF — rate control (beta-blocker / CCB / digoxin) and anticoagulate as per CHA₂DS₂-VASc score. If in doubt, treat as pre-excited AF.
Irregular Broad — Discriminator & Safety Rules
Pre-excited AF
  • Very fast (>200 bpm)
  • Varying QRS width beat-to-beat
  • History of WPW / δ wave
  • No clear BBB pattern
Torsades de Pointes
  • Twisting QRS morphology
  • Preceding long QT on ECG
  • Drug / electrolyte history
  • Self-terminating but recurrent
AF + BBB
  • Slower rate (<180 bpm)
  • Fixed BBB morphology
  • Classic RBBB / LBBB pattern
  • Known BBB or structural disease
① Stability first Unstable → synchronised DC cardioversion. If degenerated to VF → unsynchronised defibrillation + CPR.
② No AV-nodal blockers Never give adenosine, verapamil, diltiazem, beta-blockers, or digoxin to an irregular broad-complex tachycardia until pre-excited AF is excluded.
③ Deterioration risk Pre-excited AF and torsades can both degenerate to VF — have a defibrillator immediately available.
CARDIOVASCULAR__Pericarditis:
Definition & The Core Concept

Acute pericarditis = inflammation of the pericardium.

Part of a broader spectrum: acute pericarditis → effusion → tamponade, with constrictive pericarditis as the chronic sequela.
Aetiology
🦠 Infective
  • Viral (commonest) — Coxsackievirus B, enteroviruses, EBV, CMV
  • Bacterial: TB (suspect with any exudative effusion)
❤️ Post-MI
  • Early (1–3 days): fibrinous pericarditis — direct irritation
  • Late (weeks–months): Dressler's syndrome — autoimmune, fever + pleurisy
🔥 Systemic / inflammatory
  • SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, other connective tissue diseases
  • Uraemia (pericardial rub in renal failure)
  • Hypothyroidism, malignancy (lung, breast)
➕ Other
  • Radiotherapy, trauma
  • Idiopathic — the largest single group (presumed viral)
Clinical Features
💢 Chest pain — the defining symptom
  • Sharp, pleuritic, retrosternal — worse on deep inspiration + movement
  • Relieved by sitting/leaning forward (lifts the inflamed pericardium off the diaphragm)
  • Worse lying flat — key feature distinguishing it from ACS
  • Radiates to neck, left shoulder (phrenic nerve irritation)
🔊 Pericardial friction rub — the cardinal sign
  • Scratchy/squeaking, high-pitched at the left sternal edge
  • Best heard leaning forward, end-expiration
  • May be triphasic (atrial systole, ventricular systole, early diastole)
  • Transient — disappears if a large effusion develops
Systemic features: fever (esp. viral/infective), malaise, myalgia.
Diagnosis — 2 of 4 Criteria
🔶 Chest pain
  • Sharp, pleuritic, positional; relieved leaning forward
🔊 Friction rub
  • Scratchy sound at the left sternal edge
📈 ECG changes
  • Widespread saddle ST + PR depression
💧 Pericardial effusion
  • Echo-free space on TTE
≥2 of the 4 criteria = a diagnosis of acute pericarditis. TTE is recommended in all suspected cases to exclude effusion + assess myocardial involvement.
ECG in Acute Pericarditis
📈 Saddle-shaped (concave) ST elevation
  • Widespread — most leads (I, II, aVL, aVF, V2–V6)
  • Concave-upward morphology (saddle / “smiley face”)
  • Returns to baseline as inflammation resolves
  • No reciprocal ST depression
📉 PR depression — highly specific
  • Atrial epicardial involvement in inflammation
  • PR elevation in aVR (mirror image)
  • PR depression may precede ST changes
  • Other: sinus tachycardia common; low voltage if effusion develops
FeaturePericarditisSTEMI
ST shapeConcave — saddle / smileyConvex — tombstone / frowning
ST distributionWidespread — most leadsTerritorial — leads facing the infarct
Reciprocal changesAbsentPresent
PR intervalPR depression (highly specific)Normal
Q wavesNonePathological Q waves develop
EvolutionDiffuse ST → returns to baselineHyperacute T → ST rise → T inversion → Q wave
TroponinMay be mildly raised (myopericarditis)Significantly raised
Other Investigations
🔬 Workup
  • Bloods: FBC (raised WCC), CRP/ESR, U&E (uraemia), TFTs, ANA/dsDNA, troponin (myocarditis component)
  • CXR: may be normal; enlarged cardiac silhouette (effusion), pleural effusion (Dressler's)
  • TTE (echo): in all patients — exclude pericardial effusion + assess LV function
  • CT/MRI: if the diagnosis is uncertain or to assess pericardial thickening
Management
✅ First-line treatment
  • NSAIDs (ibuprofen 600 mg TDS or aspirin 750–1000 mg TDS) — continue 1–3 months
  • Colchicine 0.5 mg BD — added to the NSAID; reduces recurrence; continue 3 months
  • Taper both on symptom resolution; do not stop abruptly
  • Rest; avoid strenuous exercise until asymptomatic + CRP normalised
  • Systemic corticosteroids if an autoimmune cause (SLE/rheumatoid arthritis) or NSAID failure — use with caution
Important cautions
  • NSAIDs contraindicated post-MI — risk of myocardial rupture; use aspirin only at anti-inflammatory doses
  • Corticosteroids increase recurrence risk — only when clearly indicated
  • Anticoagulation with caution (haemopericardium risk)
Admit if high-risk features: fever >38°C, large effusion or tamponade; elevated troponin (myopericarditis); immunosuppressed or on anticoagulation; subacute onset; failure to respond to NSAIDs.
Complications: pericardial effusion (most common) · constrictive pericarditis (chronic, esp. TB) · recurrent pericarditis (>15% without colchicine) · myopericarditis.
Exam Pearls
ECG vs STEMI
Pericarditis: concave ST, widespread, PR depression, no reciprocal changes. STEMI: convex ST, territorial, reciprocal changes.
2-of-4 criteria
Chest pain · friction rub · ECG changes · pericardial effusion. Any ≥2 = diagnosis.
Post-MI caution
NSAIDs contraindicated post-MI (myocardial rupture risk); use aspirin for Dressler's.
Positional pain
Chest pain relieved by leaning forward + worse lying flat = pericarditis until proven otherwise.
Colchicine
Added to NSAIDs, halves the recurrence risk — continue 3 months.
Rub vanishes
The pericardial rub disappears when a large effusion develops — fluid separates the two inflamed layers.
Pericardial Effusion

Accumulation of fluid in the pericardial sac. Can result from any cause of pericarditis — the bridge between acute pericarditis and tamponade.

🔎 Clinical features
  • Often asymptomatic — especially if accumulation is slow
  • Effusion obscures the apex beat (fluid insulates + displaces the heartbeat)
  • Soft/muffled heart sounds
  • Dullness to percussion at the left base (Ewart's sign in large effusions — dullness below the left scapula)
  • Dyspnoea + dull retrosternal discomfort if large; symptoms of the underlying cause
📈 ECG
  • Low-voltage QRS; electrical alternans — QRS amplitude alternates beat-to-beat as the heart swings in fluid (specific for large effusion); sinus tachycardia
🩻 CXR
  • Globular (“water-bottle”) heart — flask-shaped silhouette when >250 ml; lung fields clear (unlike heart failure)
🫀 Echo (gold standard)
  • Echo-free space surrounding the heart (apical 4-chamber: a large circumferential effusion around the ventricles + atria — the diagnostic finding on TTE)
  • Quantifies size; guides pericardiocentesis; must be done urgently if tamponade suspected
Rate of accumulation determines haemodynamic impact: slow accumulation — the pericardium stretches to accommodate 1–2 L with little effect; rapid accumulation of even 150–200 ml can cause tamponade.
💊 Management
  • Treat the underlying cause — most effusions resolve with this alone
  • If symptomatic or large: pericardiocentesis (echo-guided aspiration)
  • Fluid sent for culture, cytology/histology, PCR (for TB) — highest yield with large effusions
  • If it recurs: pericardial window (excision of a pericardial segment allows ongoing drainage)
Cardiac Tamponade
A medical emergency. Pericardial fluid accumulates faster than the pericardium can stretch → rising intrapericardial pressure compresses all four chambers → impaired diastolic filling → reduced cardiac output → obstructive shock → cardiac arrest if untreated.
🔺 Beck's triad
  • Hypotension — reduced cardiac output → shock
  • Raised JVP — impaired venous return into the compressed heart
  • Muffled heart sounds — fluid surrounding + insulating the heart
➕ Additional features
  • Pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg — inspiratory fall in systolic BP (increased right-ventricular volume pushes the septum into the LV, impairing LV output)
  • Tachycardia (compensatory) + dyspnoea; cool peripheries
  • JVP: absent y descent — heart volume fixed, venous inflow can't increase in diastole
  • Kussmaul's sign absent — distinguishes it from constrictive pericarditis
🔬 Investigations
  • ECG: electrical alternans + low voltage + sinus tachycardia — the classic triad
  • CXR: large globular (water-bottle) heart; lung fields clear
  • Echo (urgent): diastolic collapse of the right atrium and/or right ventricle — the most sensitive sign; guides pericardiocentesis
Management: urgent echo-guided PERICARDIOCENTESIS — needle aspiration of pericardial fluid (cardiac arrest if not performed; immediate haemodynamic improvement expected after even small volumes are drained). Fluid analysis: culture, cytology/histology, PCR (TB). Surgical pericardial window if it recurs or the fluid is loculated.

Constrictive Pericarditis

A chronic consequence of recurrent or persistent pericarditis — the pericardium becomes a rigid fibrotic cage preventing diastolic filling. TB is the most important cause worldwide.

💧 Right-sided heart failure picture
  • Rigid pericardium traps raised venous pressure (it cannot go forward):
  • Raised JVP; dependent oedema (ankles, legs)
  • Hepatomegaly + ascites; pleural effusions
  • SOB + exercise intolerance; AF (late — atrial dilatation)
🩺 Distinctive signs
  • Kussmaul's sign — JVP paradoxically RISES on inspiration (rigid pericardium can't accommodate increased venous return)
  • Pericardial knock — loud early S3 (abrupt cessation of ventricular filling)
  • Prominent x AND y descents on JVP (contrast tamponade — y absent)
  • Normal apex beat; cannot clinically distinguish from restrictive cardiomyopathy → imaging essential
🔬 Investigations
  • CXR: normal heart size + pericardial calcification (lateral film; strongly supports the diagnosis — classically along the left lateral/inferior wall)
  • CT/MRI: pericardial thickening + calcification — gold standard for diagnosis + surgical planning
  • Echo: septal bounce, dilated IVC, preserved systolic function
  • Cardiac catheterisation: square-root sign (dip-plateau in ventricular pressure) — when imaging is inconclusive
  • Bloods: hepatic congestion pattern, hypoalbuminaemia; check for TB (Mantoux, IGRA, sputum culture)
Management: PERICARDIECTOMY (surgical excision) — the only definitive treatment; reserved for severe/progressive cases (perioperative mortality 5–15%). Bridge with diuretics for fluid overload; treat the underlying cause (TB: full anti-tuberculous therapy ± corticosteroids to reduce fibrosis); rate control for AF.
Exam Pearls
Tamponade
Beck's triad (hypotension + raised JVP + muffled sounds) + pulsus paradoxus + absent y descent → urgent echo + pericardiocentesis.
Key discriminators
Kussmaul's present in constriction, absent in tamponade; pulsus paradoxus present in tamponade, absent in constriction.
Calcification
Pericardial calcification on CXR/CT = constriction; pericardiectomy cures constriction — no surgical fix for restrictive cardiomyopathy.
Electrical alternans
QRS amplitude alternates beat-to-beat = large effusion / tamponade until proven otherwise.
Rate matters
Slow accumulation → 1–2 L tolerated; rapid → 150–200 ml can cause tamponade.
TB
The most important cause of constrictive pericarditis worldwide — always check a TB screen in an exudative effusion of unknown cause.
CARDIOVASCULAR__Infective Endocarditis:
Infective Endocarditis

Infection of the endocardium and valves; the pathological hallmark is the vegetation — a mass of platelets, fibrin, organisms and inflammatory cells.

Acute IE: fulminant (hours–days), normal/damaged valves, Staph aureus.  Subacute SBE: insidious (weeks–months), damaged valves, Strep viridans.

Strongest risk factor = previous IE. In-hospital mortality 20–30%; surgery required in ~50%.

Heart layers: endocardium (innermost) → myocardium → epicardium (visceral pericardium) → pericardial cavity → parietal pericardium → fibrous pericardium. IE infects the endocardium (inner lining).

Pathophysiology — The Three Consequence Streams

Mechanism: Endothelial damage → platelet-fibrin thrombus → pathogen seeds during bacteraemia → vegetation forms. Three consequence streams explain almost every sign:

1. Local Destruction

  • Valve regurgitation → HF
  • Annulus / aortic root abscess
  • → AV block (ECG red flag)
  • Fistula / leaflet perforation

2. Embolisation

  • Left-sided: brain, spleen, kidneys, coronary
  • Right-sided (IVDU): septic pulmonary emboli
  • Janeway lesions (painless infarcts)

3. Immune Complex Deposition

  • Small vessel vasculitis
  • Osler's nodes (painful nodules)
  • Roth spots, splinter haemorrhages
  • Glomerulonephritis (↑RF)

Systemic Infection

  • Fever (most consistent sign)
  • Malaise, night sweats, weight loss
  • Anaemia of chronic disease
  • Splenomegaly, clubbing (late/subacute)

Cardiac — Local Destruction

  • New or changing murmur (85%)
  • Signs of heart failure
  • Aortic root abscess → AV block

Embolic / Vascular Phenomena

  • Janeway lesions — painless, palms & soles
  • Stroke / TIA (left-sided)
  • Splenic, renal infarcts
  • Conjunctival haemorrhages
  • Septic pulmonary emboli (right-sided)

Immune / Vasculitic Phenomena

  • Osler's nodes — painful, finger/toe pulps
  • Roth spots (retinal, pale centre)
  • Splinter haemorrhages (subungual)
  • Glomerulonephritis (haematuria, casts)
  • Raised rheumatoid factor
Classic Exam Discrimination: Janeway = painless = embolic infarcts (palms & soles)  |  Osler's nodes = Ouch = painful = immune vasculitis (finger/toe pulps)

Persistent bacteraemia is characteristic

ECG — Serial Monitoring

New AV block → aortic root abscess — surgical emergency

Prolonging PR interval = red flag

  • Normocytic anaemia, ↑ESR/CRP, leucocytosis
  • ↑Creatinine, urine: haematuria, red cell casts
  • Raised rheumatoid factor, ↑immunoglobulins
  • Serology for culture-negative: Coxiella, Bartonella, Brucella
Red Flag: New AV block on ECG in IE = aortic root abscess until proven otherwise → urgent surgical review.
Modified Duke Criteria
Definite IE = 2 Major  |  1 Major + 3 Minor  |  5 Minor  |  Pathological proof
Major Criteria
  • Positive blood cultures: typical organism (Staph aureus, Strep viridans, Enterococcus, HACEK) in ≥2 sets; or persistently positive ≥12h apart
  • Endocardial involvement: vegetation, abscess, prosthetic dehiscence on echo; or new valvular regurgitation
Minor Criteria — BE TIMER
  • Bacteriological evidence not meeting major
  • Echo findings not meeting major
  • Temperature (fever >38°C)
  • Immune phenomena (GN, Osler's, Roth spots, +RF)
  • Microvascular / vascular phenomena (Janeway, infarcts)
  • Echo minor
  • Risk factor / predisposing condition

Principle: Prolonged IV bactericidal antibiotics — poor vascular penetration of avascular vegetation requires high drug concentrations for weeks. Take blood cultures first; discuss with microbiology.
